Sports.title: Farewell Zandvoort: Our writers' personal highlights from the F1 Dutch GP
Sports.content:
For one final time, Formula 1 cars will race around the sand dunes of Zandvoort this weekend as the seaside circuit prepares to host its final Dutch Grand Prix. After its re-entry into the calendar in 2021, the track announced its exit at the end of 2024.

Ahead of the chequered flag flying for the final time, our writers look back on some of their fondest memories from Zandvoort - including the racing action, seaside setting and vibrant orange crowds.

F1’s first non-stop nightclub

For me, the 2021 edition remains the most memorable Zandvoort experience. Nobody had thought a return to the Dutch dunes would be possible after the pinnacle of motorsport left the Netherlands following the 1985 race. That made it almost surreal to see the F1 circus descend on Circuit Zandvoort once again.

On top of that, COVID restrictions were still in place at the time, making the Dutch Grand Prix one of the first major sporting events in the country after a period in which there had been very little scope for organisers to stage anything on such a scale.

And last but not least: it was 2021, the year of one of the most intense title fights in F1 history.

On that particular Sunday in August, all those ingredients came together, especially on the grid. After the national anthem had been played and the drivers walked back to their cars to get into the zone, you could feel the tension building among everyone present.

And what best summed up the four-day festival that is the Dutch GP? The moment Verstappen put on his helmet, the DJ decided to blast ‘Super Max’ through the speakers once again – probably for the 50th time that day.

Add to that the fact that overtaking had proved difficult with the 2021 cars, meaning everything hinged on the start, while the entire orange army had turned up for just one man. The pressure on Verstappen’s shoulders was immense.

To the delight of the promoters, the Dutchman managed to withstand all that pressure and give the event its dream winner.

When then-Red Bull team principal Christian Horner left the track on Sunday evening, he aptly summed up the weekend: “It’s like I’ve been in a nightclub non-stop for four days.” With the finish line now in sight, that 2021 edition remains by far the most memorable one.

- Ronald Vording

The surprising seaside sojourn

I recall being very surprised by the news that Zandvoort was set to join the F1 calendar. Although a Dutch Grand Prix had been rumoured for some time, as the Verstappen effect set hearts in the Netherlands aflutter and the nation found renewed enthusiasm for F1, Zandvoort had been off the calendar since the end of 1985 and felt too... let's say, out of alignment with the championship's vision for no-expense-spared circuits in the desert and to suckle on the teat of developing nations with massive public investment funds. The juxtaposition of Doha and Jeddah joining the calendar at the same time as a small beach town was perceptible; it would be like if Bognor Regis suddenly found the funds to host a race...

But Zandvoort pledged to make its race different, despite the compact nature of the space available to it. Its use of banking was a smart solution and offered a very different profile to Turns 3 and 14. That, plus the festival-like nature carried into the circuit by the fans, offered personality and noise enshrouded by a smoky, orange-tinged veil.

When I covered the race with my former colleague Matt Kew in 2023, we hit upon a bit of a blinder as we found an Airbnb in Zandvoort itself. It took a brisk half-hour walk to get from the apartment to the circuit, convenient until the heavens opened on the Saturday morning. We spent the rest of the day in slightly damp clothes, as the provided umbrella offered little protection or respite...

As I've alluded to, it felt a bit incongruous to visit a race circuit, finish work for the day, and then walk five minutes to make our way to a beach restaurant for a spot of dinner. That made it all the more enjoyable, however; you value circuits that offer something a bit different, and Zandvoort certainly did so.

Watching the cars trackside was equally memorable. Seeing the drivers flirt with the outside line at the banked Turn 3 and get ever-so-close to the wall was a new experience, and meandering further down to see them scrape the floor through the kinks of Turns 5 and 6 demonstrated how hard they had to work with each lap; there wasn't really anywhere for them to relax, and a successful lap can only be achieved if a driver's truly in the rhythm.

The racing itself has been so-so - probably as you'd expect for a technical and tight circuit, although occasionally exceeding those expectations depending on the weather and the circumstance. F1's loss, then, is Formula E's gain - and I think the Gen4 machinery will excel on their seaside sojourn.

- Jake Boxall-Legge

Didier Pironi’s last victory

My earliest memories of watching televised grand prix racing are of the 1982 season. Its several tragedies were rather lost on the nine-year-old me, but throughout the early races I was captivated by the sight – more often than not, it seemed – of the two Ferraris leading while Murray Walker chirruped excitedly on the commentary.

Growing up in East Yorkshire meant the grand prix venues on UK soil were geographically rather far removed. So, as the TV coverage of the Dutch round got underway – Murray revving things up over an establishing helicopter shot of the circuit among the dunes – it was fascinating to conceive of this Zandvoort, at once entrancingly exotic and yet eminently reachable.

Summer days out in this era naturally entailed being dunked without ceremony into the bitter North Sea at wind-lashed resorts such as Bridlington or, on very special occasions, Scarborough. To think that this rarefied grand prix destination lay just over that grey horizon!

This was Didier Pironi’s last victory for Ferrari, as it turned out, before his career-ending accident, and my memory of the race is of him driving his Ferrari to its customary place in the lead early on and running unchallenged thereafter. Re-watching the BBC coverage of the race on YouTube confirmed that impression. It is the 1982 season in a microcosm: the Renaults fast but fragile; turbo-powered cars dominating in terms of laptime but often expiring in clouds of smoke; and the championship picture not quite how you recall it (John Watson leading at this point).

Older and more jaundiced eyes spot the details: ground-effect cars porpoising pendulously, little in the way of on-screen graphics, commentators who probably aren’t even trackside having to fill vast quantities of time in the absence of any on-track battles to describe. But it seemed very exciting at the time.

The following Thursday, as I read Autosport in my parents’ shop, Nigel Roebuck seemed to concur.

“After some of the places on the recent world championship schedule,” he wrote, “Zandvoort seemed like real grand prix racing again, an opportunity for cars and drivers to stretch their legs again, to get out of second gear. And perhaps our enjoyment of the place was enhanced by the fact that, until a few weeks ago, it appeared to have joined Spa, Clermont Ferrand and the Nurburgring, locked away in the vault of racing history. Going there, in the middle of the season, was like finding a bottle of Latour on a supermarket shelf.”

Given that my parents are Methodists, Nigel would have been out of luck scouting the shelves of their newsagency for fine wine. But as Zandvoort finally makes its way into the vault of history 44 years later, perhaps it’s only fitting that we should mark its passing by raising a glass of something nice.

- Stuart Codling

Cycling for fun, fried food and Formula 1

As one of the desk team at Motorsport Network, the opportunities to get out to race weekends are few and far between, which means that, more often than not, if I do go to a grand prix it’s as a paying fan. And it was as a fan that I made it to Zandvoort last year. However, because I like making things hard for myself, I decided to cycle to the race... from London.

Over three days and almost 300km, me and my party of misfits traversed the wilds of East London, the plains of East Anglia and the flats of the (west) Netherlands. There were sore legs, punctures and a few monumental downpours. But armed with a bag full of stroopwafels and fuelled by a stop at my favourite sandwich shop (Baker & Moore in Rotterdam) we edged closer to the seaside circuit. On the final approach, we joined hundreds of other riders en route, and after hurriedly tying up at the first bike park we found, we made it to the track just as FP3 kicked off.

Once there, I was sucked in by the atmosphere at the track. Sure, the lack of Max Verstappen merchandise among my party stood out in our orange grandstand, but by the fifth play through, we too were bellowing “duh duh duh duh” at the top of our lungs. The on-track action was surprisingly good that year too, with Lando Norris conking out from the race right in front of us, and Isack Hadjar clinching a glorious maiden podium.

But by the end of the weekend, what stuck with me the most was the passion of the fans, the fun that was infectious in the stands and the easy access to friet met mayonaise or kaassouffle met broodje. Zandvoort, you will be sorely missed.

- Owen Bellwood

Trendsetter for modern F1 race

There are a lot of reasons why cramped and dated Zandvoort shouldn't work for F1, but 300,000 reasons why it did. Max Verstappen's ardent fanbase turned the sleepy beach resort into a "night club", in the words of former Red Bull man Christian Horner.

That support has been unparalleled since Verstappen first burst onto the scene as a teenager, but the manner in which the Zandvoort organisers were able to corral those fans into the old school circuit and keep them entertained deserves praise.

The Dutch Grand Prix has been a trendsetter in turning a grand prix weekend into a weekend-long festival, and while some of the logistics involved remain difficult for such a small circuit, the event's heavy reliance on trains and bicycles to get fans in and out of the circuit is a case study for other promoters on the calendar.

That electric atmosphere has made Zandvoort an enjoyable race to come to, even if the on-track product hasn't always been able to keep up.

- Filip Cleeren

Sports.title: US billionaire Robert Wood Johnson acquires minor Aston Martin F1 stake
Sports.content:
Aston Martin has sold a minority stake in its Formula 1 team to US billionaire Robert Wood Johnson, who joins the board of directors as vice chairman.

Johnson, an heir of the Johnson & Johnson pharmaceutical empire, also owns the New York Jets NFL team and acquired a major stake in Premier League football team Crystal Palace last year.

The 79-year-old is a long-time donor of US president Donald Trump, and served as US ambassador to the UK between 2017 and 2021 following Trump's election.

Johnson has now been brought in by Aston owner Lawrence Stroll to advance the Silverstone team's commercial growth in the US, which is an important market for the series. The team stressed Johnson would not be involved in the team's daily management.

"During my time as US Ambassador to the United Kingdom, I have developed a deep appreciation for Aston Martin's rich history, as well as Lawrence Stroll’s strategic vision and entrepreneurial spirit," Johnson said.

"I am excited to partner with him and contribute to the continued development of the team, with the ambition of building an organisation capable of competing at the very highest level of the sport.

Lance Stroll, Aston Martin Racing Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

"We also share a commitment to growing the fanbase in the United States and introducing even more fans to the excitement of Formula 1."

Stroll added: "I am extremely happy to welcome Woody to the Aston Martin family. His experience, passion and investment further strengthen our position as we enter the next phase of our competitive journey.

"His deep appreciation for our brand, combined with his commitment to innovation and commercial opportunity, makes him an ideal partner as we look to the future.”

Sports.title: TWG denies sale of Cadillac F1 team
Sports.content:
Mark Walter might be unfamiliar in Formula 1, but for the Cadillac team, he holds fundamental relevance. The billionaire is the CEO of TWG, the company responsible for operating General Motors' Formula 1 entry, and currently he is under scrutiny by authorities in the United States which has sparked rumours regarding a potential sale of the team.

Recently, Walter sold his stake in the NBA's Los Angeles Lakers – just one year after acquiring it – while reports in the US have emerged that he is considering selling his shares in other sports ventures; including Premier League club Chelsea, MLB's Los Angeles Dodgers, and even Cadillac F1 and Andretti Global.

These moves are reportedly aimed at raising liquidity to deal with the ongoing investigation against him.

However, on Thursday at the Dutch Grand Prix, Cadillac sought to quell the speculation by stating the team was not up for sale.

Dan Towriss, Cadillac F1 team CEO, is not in attendance at Zandvoort this weekend – the first round with new team principal Marcin Budkowski at the helm - because he is with Andretti Autosport at the IndyCar race in Washington D.C., an event featuring the presence of U.S. President Donald Trump.

Read Also: Formula 1 Budkowski replaces Lowdon as Cadillac F1 boss

Marcin Budkowski, Team Principal of Cadillac F1 Team Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

TWG acquired Andretti in 2024 after purchasing the stake from Michael Andretti, a key move that allowed the FIA, F1, and rival teams to approve Cadillac’s entry as the 11th team on the grid for 2026.

What Mark Walter is accused of

Currently, the U.S. Department of Justice and the Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Mark Walter for an alleged fraud and cover-up scheme involving the management of funds at his insurance companies Delaware Life, Clear Spring, and EquiTrust.

The investigation is examining the legality of a network of undisclosed "self-loans" – estimated between $16-20billion – channelled from his insurance companies to businesses linked to the billionaire himself.

The money reportedly circulated through intermediary firms and an opaque structure of limited liability companies to evade regulatory controls and legal limits in the sector.

In the United States, companies owned by the same individual can legally lend money to one another, provided the transactions are declared to regulators to avoid compromising solvency toward customers.

Sports.title: How the 2027 F1 grid is shaping up after Verstappen's Red Bull new deal
Sports.content:
On the face of it, the emergence of three 2027 driver announcements in the same week might suggest that Formula 1's silly season had truly kicked off in style as the season emerged from its summer hibernation.

All three, however, were announcements of contract renewals. This isn't silly season - this is sensible season, and it wouldn't be wholly surprising to see news of a few more contract extensions disseminate across worldwide media platforms over the next few months. Alex Albon, Carlos Sainz, and now Max Verstappen have chosen to hold position, which should start to precipitate the fall of a few more dominoes in this year's driver market.

Read Also: Formula 1 Sainz and Albon are giving Vowles a second chance at Williams

That's not to say that the hopes of silliness are over. There's still plenty of open seats for next year and expectations of a few shuffles in the order, even if it's not the wholesale changes around the grid that perhaps some were hoping for.

Either way, 2027's grid is starting to fall into place. Here's a look at the situation so far.

Mercedes manages both Russell and Antonelli - and has both tied up for '27 Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

It's been known for quite some time that Mercedes will make no further changes to its line-up for next year - and nor does it need them.

While Kimi Antonelli's emergence as this year's title favourite will have come as some surprise to many, at least in the sense that this is only his second season, Mercedes would argue that the Italian's performances have been as forecast when it plucked him from karting and into its junior programme. Antonelli's successes have put team-mate George Russell in the shade, but the Briton is not down-and-out just yet and retains a chance of securing this year's title.

Ferrari is happy with its Leclerc-Hamilton pairing Photo by: Dom Gibbons / Formula 1 via Getty Images

Ferrari agreed a new deal with Charles Leclerc earlier this year, communicated at the start of June, as the Monegasque continues his lengthy association with the Prancing Horse on a continued multi-year basis. With Ferrari's improved performances in 2026, Leclerc's hope is that the team can press on and at last deliver a championship-winning car that chimes with his flair and all-in approach.

Lewis Hamilton mentioned earlier in the season that he too is under contract for next year. On the evidence of his performances so far over 2026, a stay at Ferrari would be much deserved; a revitalised Hamilton is second in the championship, and 50 points away from Antonelli.

One happy family? Piastri was, apparently, in no danger of leaving McLaren... Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

Both of McLaren's drivers have contracts for next year, although it was known that Verstappen had held some level of talks with the team - even if this was simply posturing to secure a more lucrative deal with Red Bull. The suggestion was that if Verstappen was to reunite with the likes of Gianpiero Lambiase and Rob Marshall, Oscar Piastri would potentially go the other way - but Piastri's manager Mark Webber shut down the idea of the Australian leaving the team a few weeks ago.

Lando Norris, meanwhile, seems content to remain a one-team man for the time being. He's been mightily impressive too, so it makes sense that McLaren would want to keep hold of the reigning champion.

Red Bull: Max Verstappen, Isack Hadjar?

Red Bull looks set to retain its full line-up for '27 after locking Verstappen down Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

Now that Verstappen is on board until at least 2030, Red Bull has its second car to sort out. This should be a mere formality, as Isack Hadjar has impressed this season and has given the Dutchman a run for his money in qualifying - even if there's a slight race-pace disparity between them.

Hadjar, out for the Dutch Grand Prix after fracturing a wrist, will keep a keen eye on Liam Lawson's return to the Red Bull fold as a substitute. However, the Frenchman shouldn't need to worry about his place in the team - unless Lawson does something really spectacular...

Could Tsolov make his F1 debut next year in a VCARB? Photo by: James Sutton / Formula 1 / Formula Motorsport Ltd via Getty Images

The first proper stop into the corridor of uncertainty lies at Racing Bulls, which may have a three-into-two-won't-go conundrum to solve. Lawson has been excellent this season and has led the line admirably for the Italian squad, while Arvid Lindblad has certainly demonstrated his credentials as a star of the future with a sensible and refreshingly self-critical approach to his rookie year.

If Red Bull's junior staircase was devoid of talent then the two would be a shoo-in to stay, but F2 championship leader Nikola Tsolov is angling to secure one of the drives for next year. Aiming to become F1's first Bulgarian driver, Tsolov has demonstrated considerable speed and his victories in both Silverstone races was a rare feature-sprint roll-over. The only hair in the soup is his occasional propensity for overly ambitious manoeuvres - as demonstrated by his clash with Sebastian Montoya in Hungary, which cost a not-insignificant points haul from the Hungaroring sprint.

Lawson will aim to use his Red Bull return as a springboard to stay with Racing Bulls, or even angle for a drive elsewhere if Tsolov and Lindblad get the nod.

Colapinto needs to keep impressing Briatore to stay at Alpine Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

Pierre Gasly signed a contract extension with Alpine last year, demonstrating his commitment to the cause despite the team being adrift at the back of the constructors' order across 2025. The arrival of Flavio Briatore, Steve Nielsen, and Mercedes has put the team back into the midfield battle, and the Frenchman is hoping that the Enstone squad can deliver a car worthy of his immense - and oft-underrated - talent.

Franco Colapinto, meanwhile, has made a considerable step in performance this year and has occasionally bested Gasly. His performances in Miami and Canada demonstrated that the Argentine is worthy of his place in F1, but needs to find greater consistency in qualifying to reduce the quantity of anonymous afternoons. Were Colapinto not to retain his place, Alpine juniors Paul Aron and Gabriele Mini would be options here.

Haas: Oliver Bearman, TBD

Bearman will stay at Haas - but who will join him? Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

With Ferrari's line-up locked in, Oliver Bearman looks set for a third full year with Haas. The Briton had an impressive start to 2026, although that form has waned as the team has gone backwards. Plagued by a handful of quality control issues and less-than-ideal gains through its development cycle, Haas is in dire need of a pick-me-up to retain seventh in the constructors' standings.

There are doubts about Esteban Ocon's place at the team, which is a shame as the Frenchman is clearly a quality driver. The problem is that, so far, the Haas move hasn't really worked for him, and the team has been cycling through a few drivers in its TPC testing to potentially identify a successor. Current reserve Ryo Hirakawa, reigning F2 champion and McLaren junior Leonardo Fornaroli, and Ferrari youngster Rafael Camara are on the list. Yuki Tsunoda was also suggested as an option, but the Japanese driver is also in talks over an IndyCar drive with Meyer Shank.

The potent Bortoleto-Hulkenberg pairing ensures Audi does not have a driver problem on its hands Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

Although Sainz was linked with Audi by some outlets, his decision to stay at Williams at least suggests that the Swiss-German team is spoken for. Bortoleto says that he's got a long-term deal in place and is expecting to stay at the team, while Hulkenberg is also understood to be in place for 2027.

There would be no reason for Audi to change its line-up, in any case; it has the perfect blend of youth and experience, and a harmonious relationship between its two team-mates.

Williams: Alex Albon, Carlos Sainz

Sainz extended his Williams deal to keep its line-up static for '27 Photo by: Andy Hone/ LAT Images via Getty Images

Williams' decision to lock in Albon and Sainz for at least another year demonstrates the buy-in for its long-term ambitions from both drivers, even if this year has presented a step back in fortunes. Some might uncharitably suggest that there was nowhere else for either driver to go, which is probably also true, but the retention of both drivers is a significant boost for the team.

Had Sainz decided to do something else, Williams is said to have hedged its bets and had spoken to the management of Sergio Perez and Colapinto for 2027, while Luke Browning has also impressed in his FP1 outings with the team.

Read Also: Formula 1 Sainz and Albon are giving Vowles a second chance at Williams

Alonso reflects on his future - will he stay at Aston Martin? Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

Stroll has effectively a life-time contract with Aston Martin, being the owner's son. Sometimes, the Canadian gives an impression of someone who doesn't really fancy being in F1 at all, but it would be surprising to see him go somewhere else.

As for the second seat, it depends on what Fernando Alonso decides to do. Adrian Newey is keen to keep the evergreen Spaniard around but, with the recent birth of his first child and continued uncertainty over the performance of the team (although the hefty Hungary package produced almost two seconds' worth of lap time), Alonso might decide to spend his 46th year around the sun doing something different. Who knows? It's up to him.

Replacements for Alonso might include whichever Racing Bulls driver misses out on a 2027 drive, Ocon, possibly Tsunoda given his Honda links, or even a promotion for Jak Crawford.

Cadillac: Sergio Perez, Valtteri Bottas?

Perez looks set to stay at Cadillac - will it keep its '26 line-up in place? Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

With the Williams avenue closed, Perez will probably stick around with Cadillac - and the American team places great value on the Mexican's inputs. Perez's attitude to the team's arrival in F1 has been refreshing; rather than be content with the team's rookie status, he seeks perfection and has consistently pushed Cadillac to iron out its key issues and find more downforce.

Bottas' rockier start to the year suggested that he might be under threat, but the Finn's performances have improved over the past few weekends as he feels more comfortable with the car. It's helped that Colton Herta's performances in F2 have not been particularly stellar, as Cadillac's dreams of promoting an American driver look to have hit a snag. Crawford might be an option, while F3 title challenger Ugo Ugochukwu might be a couple of years away from an F1 berth. Camara has also been linked to a drive with the team.

Sports.title: Sainz’s car compromised by trips through “aggressive” Zandvoort gravel in practice | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Carlos Sainz Jnr says he has had to revert to less competitive components after sustaining damage during practice for the Dutch Grand Prix.

He also indicated Williams are running low on their stock of parts as they prepare to introduce a major upgrade for their car at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix. Sainz went off three times during the first practice session which disrupted his preparations for today’s sprint race qualifying session.

“I struggled a lot this morning with the balance of the car and unfortunately went off into the gravel a few times,” said Sainz. “We damaged quite a lot of parts on the car, so in my FP1 I couldn’t run with the right components and the components that we have to put on the car for the rest of the weekend are not the best in terms of downforce and performance delivery.

“But it’s what it is. We are a bit tight on everything until we get the upgrade in Baku and unfortunately the gravel in in this track is quite aggressive and it breaks quite a lot of parts of the car. So we’ll try and learn as much as possible in the sprint and we’ll take the rest of the weekend.”

Nonetheless Sainz was pleased with his effort in qualifying for the sprint race, which left him 18th on the grid. “Obviously SQ1 is all about the first two laps,” he said, “and I didn’t get a proper read in FP1 so it’s not like I could do two very good laps because in the end you’re suffering with the lack of knowledge that you carry from FP1.

“But given how little I ran and how compromised my car is, I think I did a couple of good laps.”

After the qualifying the stewards announced Sainz is under investigation for potentially “driving unnecessarily slowly” during the session.

Sainz’s team mate Alexander Albon confirmed the team’s drivers are having to take care not to deplete their stack of spare parts. “We’ve obviously had these cars for a while now, we haven’t upgraded for a while, so they’re a little bit worse for wear, so we have to treat them nicely.”

Andrea Kimi Antonelli apologised to his team after making a mistake in the first phase of qualifying for the sprint race.

Sports.title: Engine and aerodynamic problems leave Alonso last on grid for sprint race | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Fernando Alonso will start last on the grid for the sprint race at Zandvoort after encountering multiple problems in his upgraded Aston Martin.

The team’s hopes were high for this weekend’s race after Honda brought its first upgrade for its power unit this year. But having been 12th in the opening practice session for the Dutch Grand Prix, Alonso fell to 22nd in qualifying for the sprint race.

He said he had problems with “a little bit of everything in qualifying.”

“The free practice was more or less okay but in qualifying we had problems on the engine, driveability was pushing on the braking. It was difficult to stop the car sometimes because the engine I think was over delivering

“And then apparently the SLM [straight-line mode] didn’t work for me so I could not open the rear wing So a combination of both made the laps very tricky.”

Alonso went off at Tarzan early on in the session as he struggled with the engine. “When you brake and the throttle is open, it is difficult to stop the car,” he said.

He qualified six tenths of a second slower than team mate Lance Stroll and missed the cut for the second stage of qualifying by almost 1.4 seconds.

However he remains positive about the team’s potential once it gets the best out of its latest upgrades.

“Free practice felt okay and I felt a step forward,” he said. “I think it’s very early days and probably it’s a little bit immature with all the controls, et cetera.

“It’s a sprint weekend: on a normal weekend we have three practices to nail the package, obviously on a sprint we need to deal with the situation in today’s qualifying and tomorrow on the sprint race we’ll try to understand also a few things.”

Sports.title: Russell takes sprint race pole position, Antonelli fifth after error in SQ1 | Formula 1
Sports.content:
George Russell will start the sprint race at Zandvoort from pole position, four places ahead of the championship leader.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli could only manage fifth on the grid after making a mistake at the beginning of the session.

Lando Norris, the most recent race-winner, will join Russell on the front row of the grid. The two Mercedes drivers will also be separated by Charles Leclerc and Oscar Piastri.

Antonelli at least managed to out-qualify his closest championship rival, Lewis Hamilton. The Ferrari driver complained Max Verstappen held him up in SQ1 but the stewards decided no investigation was necessary. Verstappen pipped Hamilton to sixth on the grid.

Antonelli had a scare in the first part of qualifying: he was still in the drop zone with three-and-a-half minutes. He went off at turn 13 on his first run and although he avoided any significant damage to his car it left him needing a late flying lap to secure his place in SQ2.

The two drivers in unfamiliar cars – Liam Lawson at Red Bull and Yuki Tsunoda at Racing Bulls – posted near-identical times in SQ2, missing the cut for the final 10 by three-tenths of a second. Arvid Lindblad’s final effort prevented his usual team mate Lawson from reaching SQ3 in his Red Bull.

Franco Colapinto, who unlike Pierre Gasly did not have the new parts on his Alpine, qualified 13th. Nico Hulkenberg failed to join his Audi team mate in SQ3, while Esteban Ocon and Alexander Albon left their team mates behind in the first round.

Neither of the upgraded Aston Martin-Hondas made it into SQ2. Fernando Alonso locked up heavily at Tarzan on a early lap and ran through the gravel. His Straight Line Mode did not work on his final run, leaving him last on the grid. Both Cadillac drivers also went out in the first round.

Sports.title: Antonelli leads Norris in Zandvoort practice, no Red Bulls in top 10 | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli headed the sole practice session for the Dutch Grand Prix.

Hungarian Grand Prix winner Lando Norris split the two Mercedes drivers at the top of the times at the end of the single hour of running at Zandvoort.

Rain before the session began left the track damp but drying as the session started. Although the first drivers to join the track used intermediate tyres they quickly decided it was ready for slicks.

Antonelli was the first of the front-runners to set a competitive time. The Mercedes and Ferrari drivers exchanged the quickest times on the harder rubber.

Drivers switched to the soft tyres with 10 minutes to go in order to simulate their qualifying runs. The Ferrari drivers briefly led the way, then Norris narrowly beat Lewis Hamilton.

Antonelli’s first attempt at a qualifying run was spoiled when he encountered Nico Hulkenberg’s Audi during his lap. However his soft rubber proved capable of performing another run and the world championship leader duly dipped under the 1’13 mark, setting a best time of 1’12.949.

No one else could match that. Norris also improved his time but ended up a tenth of a second behind Antonelli, leading the other Mercedes of George Russell by a mere four thousandths of a second.

The Ferrari pair came next, followed by Oscar Piastri in the other McLaren. Neither Red Bull appeared in the top 10, Max Verstappen struggling with oversteer on his way to the 11th-fastest time.

Liam Lawson was half a second slower than Max Verstappen on his return to Red Bull. Isack Hadjar, whose seat Lawson has temporarily taken over, appeared at the track with his injured wrist during the session.

Audi showed strong pace again, Nico Hulkenberg setting the seventh fastest time. He was separated from his team mate by Pierre Gasly, who is the only Alpine driver to benefit from the team’s upgrade package this weekend.

Arvid Lindblad completed the top 10, nine-tenths of a second quicker than the returning Yuki Tsunoda in the other Racing Bulls. Honda’s new power unit helped Fernando Alonso to 12th in the times sheets behind Verstappen.

Sports.title: Featured Comment: Why didn’t Verstappen leave Red Bull? | Brief
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen won four world championships in a row at Red Bull but the team’s form has been on a downward trajectory since the middle of 2024. Many of their top staff have left and they haven’t won a race so far this year.

So why did Verstappen decide now is the right time to renew his contract?

I think Verstappen seriously wanted to leave, but there was no place for him to go. Mercedes would have been his number one choice, but Wolff probably saw too much risk in a Verstappen/Antonelli pairing. I am sure McLaren would have taken Verstappen for Piastri, but McLaren is too much of a sideways step for Verstappen. Taking on a challenge like Aston Martin has too much danger of sidelining his career and leaving him in an Alonso state. So a contract extension with favorable exit clauses makes the most sense at the moment. See what openings are available in a year or two.

Sports.title: Verstappen considered leaving F1 before deciding to renew Red Bull deal | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen says he considered whether he wanted to keep racing in Formula 1 before deciding to sign a new deal to drive for Red Bull.

The team today announced an extension to his previous deal which ran to 2028. Verstappen will remain at Red Bull until at least 2030.

Verstappen has been an outspoken critic of F1’s power unit regulations. The sport will introduce revisions to them over the coming seasons but significant change is not possible before 2030. However Verstappen said he is prepared to tolerate the situation until then.

He said his uncertainty early in the year was “mainly about actually continuing in Formula 1.”

“But the rules are slowly getting a bit better and, let’s say, I’m willing to live with it. And hopefully by 2030 it opens up another opportunity, potentially with V8 engines coming in, to look again.”

Verstappen has begun competing in other series alongside his F1 commitments, including the Nurburgring 24 Hours earlier this year. He said he intends to continue racing in other championships.

“For me that was definitely something that I want to keep doing,” he said. “But, of course, it depends a bit on the F1 calendar, what will be possible also next year.”

He is most interested in entering “all the big endurance ones – 24-hour races in general, they would be cool to drive in.”

As Red Bull’s form has dipped in recent seasons, Verstappen has been tipped as a target for rival teams such as Mercedes and McLaren. When asked, Verstappen did not deny his management had spoken with rival teams, replying: “it doesn’t matter”.

Sports.title: Jahmal Harvey Crushes Keb With Second-Round Knockout
Sports.content:
The punishment continued in the second round. Harvey hurt Keb with a fast combination before landing a crushing right cross that sent him heavily to the canvas and ended the scheduled six-round contest.

The punch statistics showed how one-sided the fight had been. Harvey landed 46 of 84 power punches for a 55 percent connect rate, including 37 shots to the head. Keb connected with only 10 of 44 power punches and landed seven to the head.

Those numbers also raise the question of how quickly MVP will advance Harvey. The 23-year-old was a 2021 amateur world champion and reached the quarterfinals at the Paris Olympics, giving him far more experience than his four professional fights suggest.

Another opponent at Keb’s level will not reveal much. Harvey needs someone capable of surviving his early speed, forcing him to adjust, and making him work through difficult rounds. His amateur background and rapid start leave little reason to move him at the pace of an ordinary prospect.

The knockout was the strongest performance of Harvey’s young professional career, but the ease of the win made the matchmaking look too safe. His next opponent should offer enough resistance to show how close Harvey is to facing established lightweights.

The bout served as the co-feature of the Amanda Serrano versus Lucrecia Manzur card and streamed free on TikTok LIVE.

Sports.title: Amanda Serrano vs. Lucrecia Manzur Live Results and Fight Updates
Sports.content:
Jahmal “Hard Rock” Harvey (4-0, 3 KOs) scored a brutal second-round knockout of Hammet Kowany Keb del Valle (7-3-1, 6 KOs) in the lightweight co-feature. The 2024 U.S. Olympian controlled the fight from the opening bell with his speed and accuracy. Harvey hurt Keb with a sharp combination in the second before finishing him with a crushing right cross. The punch dropped the Mexican heavily and ended the contest. Harvey recorded the most impressive finish of his young professional career.

Melissa Mortensen (10-0, 5 KOs) defeated Mayelli Flores Rosquero (13-3-1, 4 KOs) by split decision to claim the vacant WBA super bantamweight title. Flores scored a flash knockdown in the second round, but Mortensen controlled most of the remaining action. The taller, younger Dane was busier and repeatedly caught Flores with clean punches as the Mexican pressed forward. Although the crowd loudly booed the outcome, Mortensen deserved the decision and won more rounds. Two judges scored it 95-94 for Mortensen, while the third had Flores ahead 95-94.

Avious “The Underdog” Griffin (20-1, 19 KOs) stopped Jackson “El Fenix” Marinez (23-5, 11 KOs) after five rounds of their welterweight bout. Marinez pressed forward and found success with his jab while Griffin started slowly. Griffin gradually closed the distance and began overpowering the Dominican veteran. Two left hooks and a right hand produced the first knockdown in the fifth, before an overhand right and left hook to the body sent Marinez down again. Marinez’s corner stopped the fight before the sixth round began.

Cinderella Linnear (2-0) upset Jully “Poca” De Oliveira (1-1) by split decision after four competitive rounds. The two light welterweights fought a close contest with little separating them. Two judges awarded Linnear the fight by scores of 39-37. The third judge scored it 39-37 for Oliveira. Some observers believed the bout was even or felt Oliveira had done enough to win.

Keno Marley (3-0, 2 KOs) stopped Braylan Brooks (1-1, 1 KO) in the third round of their cruiserweight bout. The 6-foot-3 Brazilian used his height and boxing skills to control the action. Brooks struggled to close the distance or disrupt Marley’s rhythm. Marley increased the pressure and forced the stoppage during the third. The two-time Olympian secured his second knockout in three professional fights.

Brook “Mighty” Sibrian (10-3, 4 KOs) upset Guadalupe Medina (12-1, 3 KOs) by unanimous decision after eight action-packed rounds. Sibrian applied relentless pressure and repeatedly attacked Medina’s body. Her higher output kept the favored prospect from controlling the pace. The judges scored the minimumweight fight 78-74, 78-74, and 77-75. Sibrian earned a clear decision and handed Medina her first professional defeat.

Iyana “Roxy” Verduzco (8-0, 1 KO) edged Miguelina Hernandez (4-1, 3 KOs) by split decision after eight competitive rounds. Neither fighter established clear control in a closely contested bout. Two judges favored Verduzco by scores of 77-75 and 78-74. The remaining judge scored it 78-74 for Hernandez. Some observers believed Hernandez deserved the decision or had done enough to earn a draw.

Nelvie Tiafack (5-0, 4 KOs) overwhelmed Salvador Zavala Molina (7-1, 5 KOs) in a heavyweight mismatch that ended in the third round. The stronger Tiafack controlled the opening two rounds before sharply increasing his output in the third. Zavala fought back but was reduced to survival mode as Tiafack unloaded with heavy punches. No knockdown occurred before the referee stopped the contest. The finish looked slightly early, but Zavala was taking punishment with little chance of changing the fight.

Albina Moldazhanova knocked out Sheila Fabiana Liesegang in the first round of their light welterweight bout. The Russian southpaw Moldazhanova (5-0, 5 KOs) attacked early and dropped Liesegang (6-1, 4 KOs) before the fight could settle into a rhythm. Liesegang was unable to beat the referee’s count. The knockout came at 1:21 of the opening round. All five of Moldazhanova’s professional victories have ended inside the distance.

Jocelyn Camarillo (7-0, 1 KO) used her speed, movement, and clean punching to control Ashley Felix (7-5, 1 KO) over six rounds. She repeatedly stepped into range with sharp shots before moving away from Felix’s counters. Felix had brief success but struggled to sustain her offense. The judges scored the minimumweight bout 58-56, 59-55, and 60-54.

Paolo Barredo outboxed Jorge Garcia over six rounds to earn a unanimous decision in their lightweight bout. Barredo (7-0, 2 KOs) controlled most of the action but was unable to stop the heavier-punching Mexican Garcia (3-2, 3 KOs). The judges scored it 60-54, 59-55 and 59-55.

Amanda Serrano fights Lucrecia Manzur tonight, Friday, August 21, at Pechanga Resort Casino, with their ring walks expected around 11:30 p.m. ET. The main card starts at 7 p.m. ET / midnight UK.

Sports.title: Bradley Questions Ryan Garcia But Gives Benn A Pass
Sports.content:
“You want to be a fighter or you want to be a social media darling? Pick one. Boxing gets jealous. Your mitt work, I’m looking at it like, ‘Where is the intensity?’ There ain’t no intensity in that. Have a real camp. I hope this is just for the people and you’re not really showing what you’re doing,” Bradley said on his channel.

A short training clip does not reveal everything Garcia is doing. Bradley also fails to give Ryan credit for redeeming himself against Mario Barrios in his last fight. Garcia arrived in good condition, remained composed and showed that the Rolando Romero loss had not destroyed him.

Rolly presented a different physical threat. He looked enormous inside the ring and repeatedly threw double left hooks that rattled Garcia. Ryan seemed to underestimate Romero’s size and power, then failed to adjust once those hooks began landing.

Against Regis Prograis, Benn struggled throughout, taking shots and unable to hurt him. He came down to 150 pounds for their April catchweight fight and absorbed plenty of punishment despite winning a 10-round unanimous decision.

Making the 147-pound welterweight limit requires Benn to drop three additional pounds. That cut may reduce his strength, punch resistance and ability to maintain pressure.

Pressure remains Benn’s best method of testing Garcia by attacking early and denying him room, but rushing forward carries danger. Ryan owns the faster hands and the left hook smash that he’s known for. Romero’s double left hook troubled him because it was delivered by a much larger man with unusual power. Benn may not carry the same force at 147.

By studying Ryan’s social media clips, Bradley is giving Benn the benefit of the doubt. Their recent performances provide a different picture: Garcia responded well against Barrios, while Benn endured a punishing night at a weight three pounds above the one he must reach in Las Vegas.

Sports.title: WBA Welterweight Title Clash Rolly vs Teofimo
Sports.content:
Throughout his pro career, Rolly Romero was categorized as a hard-hitting puncher who possessed limited boxing skills. He was in the process of building a solid career, but in May 2025, Romero earned a signature win.

As the challenger, Rolly Romero had a big moment when he knocked down Ryan Garcia in the second round. Romero displayed poise and ring generalship as he outpointed Garcia and won the WBA welterweight title.

When it comes to a signature win, Rolly Romero’s upcoming opponent is very familiar with that term. Teofimo Lopez is a boxer who has not one but two certified signature wins.

Back in October 2020, Lopez executed his game plan to perfection as he outboxed a prime Vasiliy Lomachenko. Three years later, Lopez put on another masterclass as he dominated Josh Taylor and won the Ring and the WBO 140-pound world titles.

Lopez would go on to have three successful title defenses. The night of January 31, 2026, was a rough night for Lopez due to the fact that Shakur Stevenson was able to control distance, dictate the pace of the bout, and, as a result, he cruised to a unanimous decision victory.

Now the former two-division world champion Teofimo Lopez will attempt to bounce back in a big way. Lopez will step in the ring and attempt to defeat his close friend and become a three-division world champion.

Teofimo is a boxer-puncher who is explosive, athletic, and a dangerous counterpuncher. Rolly is awkward, but he’s an aggressive fighter who is accustomed to pressing forward and landing power shots from unexpected angles.

When it comes to pure boxing, Teofimo has the advantage. When it comes down to punching power, you have to give the advantage to Rolly.

To win this fight, Teofimo Lopez has to utilize his advantage, which is his skill set. He has to use his jab, control distance, be defensively responsible, and outbox the heavy-handed Romero.

Rolly Romero has to show the poise and discipline he displayed in the fight against Ryan Garcia. He has to set up his shots, because one of his power shots can change the complexion of the fight.

On the night of August 22nd, the question is, will Teofimo Lopez add to his legacy by becoming a three-division world champion, or will Rolly Romero enhance his resume by taking down his second boxing star in a row?

Sports.title: Emiliano Vargas Claims He Is Ready For Shakur
Sports.content:
“I’m a fighter. I’d want to fight him tomorrow. But at the end of the day, we’ve got to see what’s going on, if he’s going to continue with the belt or relinquish it because of the fact that he’s with Zuffa now. I think it’s the time for me to fight for a world title,” said Emiliano to Sean Zittel.

Recent sparring with Teofimo Lopez convinced Vargas that he can compete at championship level. He also referred to previous work with Jorge Linares as another source of confidence.

Gym sessions with accomplished fighters can help his development, but they do not answer the questions created by his matchmaking. Headgear, larger gloves, and controlled rounds cannot reproduce the consequences of facing a rival intent on taking his position.

Ernesto “Tito” Mercado has repeatedly called for a fight with Vargas. Mercado publicly identified him as one of the opponents he wanted as recently as June, when Vargas was ranked No. 2 by the WBO. Vargas did not mention Mercado by name while declaring that he would face anyone in the top 10.

Facing Mercado would provide the type of test Vargas needs before challenging Shakur. His power and pressure would examine the young fighter in ways Bryce Mills and Agustin Ezequiel Quintana did not. A fight with Shakur would be an even greater leap. Vargas has not faced anyone possessing his speed, defensive ability, timing, or championship experience. Shakur would receive heavy criticism from fans if he selected Vargas as his next opponent. At 22, Vargas has been positioned for a title fight without defeating a leading light welterweight. His WBO ranking would not prevent the matchup from being viewed as another favorable choice.

The reaction would be stronger after Shakur demanded a 144-pound catchweight for a proposed fight with Devin Haney, a condition that helped sink those negotiations. Following that breakdown, fans would expect him to face an established 140-pounder or a major opponent moving up from lightweight.

Without beating Mercado or another leading contender, Vargas would look undeserving of a title fight after facing someone at Bryce Mills’ level. The WBO ranking places Vargas within reach of the champion. His opposition has not shown that he belongs there.

Sports.title: Rolly Romero Goes Silent After Making Weight
Sports.content:
Tim Bradley Is Judging The Wrong Rolly And Teofimo

Tim Bradley sees Rolly Romero as little more than a puncher and expects Teofimo Lopez’s superior speed, skill and counterpunching to turn Saturday night’s welterweight fight into a mismatch.

That view depends on Rolly remaining the same limited fighter he was in the past and Teofimo returning to the form that carried him to the top at lightweight. Neither view looks safe.

“This ain’t even going to be close. This is a damn mismatch, man,” Bradley said on his channel. “Natural instincts, fast-twitch muscles, speed, power, counterpunching ability. He about to smoke Rolly Romero. For real, y’all banking on a miracle for Rolly. Seriously, he got a puncher’s chance. That’s it.”

Bradley still sees the wild and defensively vulnerable Rolly who lost to Gervonta Davis and Isaac Cruz. He also seems to picture Teofimo as the same fighter that defeated the older, smaller Vasiliy Lomachenko at 135 pounds in 2020. He hasn’t looked like that fighter since his loss to George Kambosos Jr. five years ago. Moving up in weight to 140 took away what made Teofimo successful. His size advantage over his opposition.

Rolly has filled out and looks like a genuine welterweight at this point in his career, and he looks younger at 30. Although Lopez is a year younger at 29, he appears older. Some of that could be the grueling fights he’s had during his career beginning to show,

Size-wise, Teofimo still resembles a lightweight fighting above his natural division. His power did not carry cleanly to 140, and moving up another seven pounds will not restore it. He’d been able to disguise the lack of size with the opposition he’s been matched against. Teo wasn’t put in there with the likes of Oscar Duarte, Keyshawn Davis, Richardson Hitchins, Ernesto Mercado or Andy Hiraoka.

Easy work is what Bradley expects if the Teofimo who defeated Barboza turns up. That version may not be enough against a naturally bigger man who can take his punches and hurt him in return. The flaws Teofimo managed at 140 may become far more costly at 147.

Moving up still makes financial sense. The most valuable fights are there, and beating Rolly would place Lopez near Devin Haney, Conor Benn and a Ryan Garcia fight. A defeat may not eliminate those possibilities because his name and accomplishments at lightweight and light welterweight retain value. This is a profitable risk for Teofimo. Bradley is taking a different one by trusting a picture of both fighters that may no longer exist.

Sports.title: Fury Accuses Joshua And Hearn Of Greed
Sports.content:
“Doesn’t look like they’re going to sign the fight, and it doesn’t look like it’s going to happen, all because Eddie and AJ want more money. They’ve already had that much money off Turki in the last few years. They’ve had boxing deals. They’ve had darts deals,” said Fury on social media. “They’ve had snooker deals. They’ve had everything. Yet they’ve got the audacity and cheek to ask for more money from old Turki. I tell you what, it’s disgusting.”

The attack was crude, but Fury made a point that is likely to connect with fans who have watched Joshua receive enormous Saudi-backed opportunities. Joshua faced Otto Wallin in Riyadh in December 2023, returned for the Francis Ngannou event there the following year, and later fought Daniel Dubois at Wembley Stadium on another Alalshikh-backed card.

Hearn has also developed a wider business relationship with Saudi organizers through Matchroom’s boxing events. Fury argued that Joshua and his promoter have already benefited heavily from Alalshikh’s investment but are still demanding better terms before accepting the biggest fight available to them.

“All this talk of, ‘We want the fight in England, we want this, we want that.’ It’s only to get more money to go to America,” Fury said. “Look at the money you have had off Turki, and yet you’re still asking to do darts deals and snooker deals off the back of my fight.”

The unusual part is that Fury sounds content with his offer. He says he will go wherever Alalshikh and Zuffa want to stage the fight without demanding a location premium. Joshua and Hearn are the ones pushing for more money and allowing the venue issue to delay the agreement.

“I bent over backwards to make this fight happen,” Fury said. “First of all, it was in England. Then it was in Ireland. Then it was in America. I said, ‘I’ll go anywhere. I’m not interested where the fight is. I just want to fight.’”

That willingness places Fury in a strong position from which to scold Joshua. He can portray himself as the cooperative fighter who accepted the money, the location, and every party involved. Joshua is left looking as if he risks endangering a long-awaited event by demanding a larger purse to travel to New York.

A British stadium may be Joshua’s preference, but that location does not serve Alalshikh’s plans or Netflix’s interest in staging the fight during American prime time. Madison Square Garden also gives Zuffa a valuable platform for placing its fighters on the undercard as the company moves deeper into boxing.

With the amount Alalshikh has invested in Joshua, asking him to accept New York does not sound unreasonable. It would be a reciprocal gesture toward the financier who made the event possible and supported several of Joshua’s largest paydays.

The former champion would not be fighting in obscurity or surrendering his place in the promotion. Madison Square Garden remains one of boxing’s most prestigious venues, and Netflix would place the fight before a large American audience.

Even if Alalshikh grants every request in Hearn’s addendum and gives Joshua a substantial financial bump, the immediate gain could carry a much larger cost. Their relationship with Alalshikh has already generated far more than the earnings from one event.

Alalshikh can accept their demands and still take a different view of future business with Joshua and Matchroom. Other fighters and promoters are competing for the same financial backing, dates, and opportunities. Making this agreement unnecessarily difficult gives him little reason to remain as accommodating the next time.

Joshua and Hearn have every right to negotiate the best terms available. How far they should press the person financing the fight and creating another enormous payday for Joshua is another matter.

Fury’s account has not been supported with purse figures, contracts, or a detailed response from Joshua’s team. A significant change from a British stadium to Madison Square Garden can justify renegotiating parts of the deal. How much Joshua should require before helping Alalshikh deliver an event that benefits Netflix and Zuffa is less clear.

An improved offer may settle the dispute, but it will not answer the larger question. After everything Alalshikh has made possible for Joshua and Hearn, where is the thank you?

Sports.title: Bill Haney’s Riyadh Plan Fails To Deliver Ryan Garcia
Sports.content:
“We also went on the undercard in a belief that we would be helping the overall mission to have Devin and Ryan Garcia in there for a fight,” Bill told the Mr. Verzace podcast. “I no longer believe that that’s the mission. I’ve unloosed the team and told them, ‘Listen, we’re fighting main event and we don’t give a [expletive] who we fight.’”

That change is not encouraging for the Haneys. Ryan’s September 12 fight with Conor Benn is being presented by Zuffa Boxing and The Ring, with Turki Alalshikh involved. The groups controlling the event may have different plans for the winner.

At 147 pounds, Ryan has no shortage of marketable opponents. An entertaining fight with Benn can lead to a rematch. A Rolly Romero victory over Teofimo Lopez would create interest in Garcia trying to avenge his 2025 loss. Teofimo beating Rolly opens another major fight.

Three more possibilities are Richardson Hitchins, Keyshawn Davis, and Shakur Stevenson, all of whom would welcome the chance to face Garcia. Devin is one of at least six names competing for Ryan’s attention.

His performance against Brian Norman Jr. did little to make him indispensable. Devin secured the belt with a cautious approach, repeatedly clinching when Norman reached punching distance. He won, but the minimalist style was not a strong  for another major investment. Turki has previously criticized low-action fights after watching Devin defeat Jose Ramirez in Times Square. With several action-oriented rivals available for Garcia, financing the Haney rematch may not be his first choice.

Waiting for the Saudis to handle the matchmaking is no longer enough. Bill needs to contact IBF champion Liam Paro or WBA regular champion Jack Catterall and complete a deal while either remains available.

Interest from Paro’s team did not produce an offer. Catterall accepted a proposed date and Atlanta location before communication from Devin’s side stopped. The opportunity may soon disappear because the WBA mandatory can pursue the winner of Rolly versus Teofimo rather than wait for the Haneys to return his call.

Remaining inactive does not reserve Devin’s place opposite Garcia. It gives Ryan’s other possibilities time to become more valuable and allows Paro and Catterall to make plans without him.

Riyadh did not provide the matchmaking help Bill expected. His job now is to keep Devin active before Garcia and the available alternatives move beyond him.

Ghana News.title: ‘The Big Push is pushing’ – Upper West MPs hail contractors delivering in the region
Ghana News.content:
"The Big Push is pushing."

That was the verdict as the Upper West Parliamentary Caucus inspected roads under President John Dramani Mahama’s flagship infrastructure agenda on Thursday, August 20.

Their message after a day on the ground: Praise for contractors who are delivering, pressure for those behind schedule, and a promise from the contractor that work will be done by 2028.

Leading the team, Caucus Leader Dr. Sebastian Sandaare said the visit to the Mwankuri-Han and the Han-Nandawwaala-Kuntulo- Jeffisi-Tumu portions was to verify work on the ground. The project has been awarded to five contractors.

"These are roads under His Excellency John Dramani Mahama that have been awarded under the Big Push. We are here to see for ourselves what is happening. After this, we will report our observations to the Minister of Roads," he said.

"What we want is for the roads to be done on time and to be of good quality. You know how we struggle and how bad our roads are. Our people are crying for quality work, and the work should also be completed on time.

P&W Ghanem Limited received the flowers and special praise.

Lawra MP Bede A. Ziedeng commended the contractor for "neat" and "fast" work.

"Those who cannot do the work, let’s take the contract from them and give to people who can do it. Without this road, Upper West will continue to suffer," Nadowli-Kaleo MP Anthony Sumah Mwinkaara was specific.

"He has done the prime on one side and is just two kilometres away from putting the second seal. The entire stretch here has the second seal done. At the rate he is going, he is the only one we are sure will finish before time."

Wa West MP, Supt. Retired Peter Lanchene Toobu wrapped up the caucus remarks.

"P&W Ghanem is showing class. He's showing speed. He's showing competence. If all the contractors were working like this, I am quite convinced nobody in the region would be raising issues about delays. So far, so very good."

"We have told them that some of them are behind schedule, and we expect them to speed up, to double up.

Briefing the MPs, Caesar Ghanem, the CEO of P&W Ghanem, explained the scope.

"The first project runs from Manco Reef and it is 22 kilometers. So far we have completed the prime seal. We are currently doing the first seal, and we still have to do the second seal. In total it will be three layers," he said. He said the second project covers 25 kilometers: 15km from Nandom towards Lawra and 10km from Nandom towards Lambussie.

"So far we have completed the fill formation. Currently we are preparing for the sub-base. Hopefully next week we will start that layer, then the base, and then the seal work."

On timelines, he was confident.

"The project is expected to be completed before the deadline, which is January or February 2028. Each project has a duration of two years. As you can see, the first project has been sealed almost entirely. The remaining work will not take much time." He added that the overlay of asphalt promised by the Roads Minister will come under a separate contract.

"For now, this contract covers three layers of surface dressing: prime seal and first seal."

The caucus also visited the site of Greenhouse limited at the Kuntulo stretch heading to Jeffisi to see the progress of work.

Lawra MP, Bede Ziedeng also commented on P&W Ghanem’s work on the Han-Domini-Lawra Road, where sub-base works are complete.

For road users, the impact is already real. Mr Hudu Nafa says his trip from Wa to Tumuh has been transformed.

"I used to take four to five hours. But now, I've only used one hour and twenty minutes. The road is very nice."



"Let's give thanks and praises, and we'll continue to vote for the government. We are only appealing that they should continue with the rest of the road. From Kanyininguase to Wa is the only place that is not good for us now." Nurudin Saani of the NHIA agreed.

"Previously the road was very terrible. You could use almost four hours to Wa. Now I used two hours. When JM was saying it, a lot of people had doubts. But it has really come to reality."

Nadowli-Kaleo MP Anthony Sumah raised concerns about deteriorating sections.

"From Magazine down to Jang, it is so bad. This is a place that was tarred initially, but it has gone very bad. We cannot be building new roads and neglecting the old ones that need maintenance. If the contractor does not come on site, we will meet with the Minister and suggest decisive action," he said.

Ghana News.title: Government sets up team to negotiate VALCO strategic partnership
Ghana News.content:
The government has taken a major step towards reviving the Volta Aluminium Company Limited (VALCO), inaugurating a dedicated team to negotiate with a prospective strategic investor to modernise and expand the Tema-based aluminium smelter.

The eight-member Negotiations Team, inaugurated by the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources on Friday, August 21, 2026, is expected to work towards securing definitive terms for a partnership that will provide the capital and technical support required to restore VALCO’s productive capacity.

The initiative forms part of efforts to reposition the company as an efficient, commercially viable and globally competitive player in Ghana’s aluminium industry while safeguarding the country’s strategic interests in the sector.

Inaugurating the team, the Minister for Lands and Natural Resources, Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah, said the government remained committed to ensuring the survival and long-term sustainability of VALCO.

He charged members of the team to approach the negotiations with transparency, diligence and a strong focus on value for money.

The Minister stressed that VALCO was too important to Ghana’s industrialisation ambitions to be allowed to collapse.

The negotiations will, among other things, examine the technical capabilities, financial strength, smelter-operating experience and long-term investment plans of prospective partners.

The objective is to identify an investor capable of providing the resources needed to rehabilitate the smelter and support its expansion.

The move comes against the backdrop of growing operational difficulties at VALCO.

The number of active cells at the smelter has declined from 127 in 2025 to about 90 as of August 2026.

The decline has been attributed to ageing equipment, power constraints and supply chain difficulties, all of which have affected the company's ability to operate at its intended capacity.

The government has, however, sought to reassure workers and other stakeholders that bringing in a strategic investor should not be interpreted as an outright sale of the company.

Rather, the proposed arrangement is expected to involve a credible investor providing capital for retooling and modernisation while helping to secure VALCO’s future and protect jobs.

The Negotiations Team brings together representatives of key institutions with an interest in the future of the aluminium industry.

Its membership includes officials from the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources, the Ghana Integrated Aluminium Development Corporation (GIADEC), the Ministry of Finance, the Attorney-General’s Department and VALCO.

The team will therefore be required to balance commercial considerations with legal, financial, industrial and national-interest concerns as negotiations progress.

VALCO occupies a significant place in Ghana’s industrial history.

Established in 1964 as part of the post-independence industrialisation programme under President Kwame Nkrumah, the company was conceived as a cornerstone of an integrated aluminium industry.

The Tema smelter was designed to operate more than 200 pots and produce up to 200,000 tonnes of aluminium annually, using electricity generated from the Akosombo Dam.

At its peak, VALCO was a major industrial employer and an important source of foreign exchange for the country.

The government subsequently acquired all the shares in VALCO in 2008 following the exit of Kaiser Aluminium.

Since then, the company has faced persistent challenges, including high and unstable electricity costs, ageing infrastructure and inadequate capital for large-scale rehabilitation.

Efforts to bring in a strategic investor have been underway for several years.

In 2022, Cabinet approved a request by GIADEC and VALCO to pursue a strategic equity investor to support the modernisation of the smelter.

A technical and financial assessment undertaken by KPMG that year subsequently recommended equity investment as the most commercially viable option for restoring VALCO.

In November 2025, the government constituted a 12-member cross-sectoral committee to assess proposals from prospective investors.

The committee, comprising representatives of VALCO, GIADEC and various government ministries, submitted its options analysis report on January 7, 2026.

GIADEC, which was established in 2018 to spearhead the development of Ghana’s integrated bauxite-to-aluminium value chain, has maintained that the government's objective is not to dispose of VALCO outright.

Under the proposed partnership model, the State would give up a portion of its equity to a strategic investor in return for the capital injection required to modernise the smelter.

Ghana News.title: Ghana clears upstream disputes as $3.5bn investment pipeline takes shape
Ghana News.content:
Emeafa Hardcastle

Ghana’s upstream petroleum industry is poised for a fresh wave of investment after the government resolved outstanding disputes with key oil and gas operators, removing a major source of uncertainty that had weighed on investor confidence.

The development, according to the Chief Executive Officer of the Petroleum Commission, Emeafa Hardcastle, has created a more predictable operating environment and opened the way for new capital to flow into the sector.

She said the resolution of the disputes was consistent with the government’s commitment to creating certainty for investors and ensuring that Ghana’s petroleum resources continued to generate greater economic value.

“Pursuant to the promise His Excellency made to Ghanaians, all disputes between upstream oil and gas players and the government of Ghana have been promptly resolved, paving the way for more investment,” she said.

Madam Hardcastle made the disclosure in Accra at the launch of the 2025 Annual Investment Report, where she outlined developments shaping investment in Ghana’s upstream petroleum industry.

She said the improved investment climate was already translating into concrete financial commitments from major industry players.

According to her, partners in the Jubilee and TEN fields have committed US$2 billion to further development activities.

The investment is expected to support increased oil production and boost gas output, while also contributing to a reduction in the Jubilee gas price.

Madam Hardcastle said the expected reduction in the Jubilee gas price was about 18 per cent, which could result in savings of approximately US$300 million for Ghana.

The commitment is significant for Ghana as the country seeks to maximise production from existing fields while strengthening the role of domestic gas in the energy sector.

$1.5bn gas expansion

The Petroleum Commission CEO also disclosed another major investment commitment from the Offshore Cape Three Points partners.

She said Eni, Vitol and the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation (GNPC) had pledged US$1.5 billion towards expanding gas exports and developing the Eban-Akoma discoveries.

Together, the two commitments amount to about US$3.5 billion, signalling renewed interest in Ghana’s upstream petroleum potential.

The investments are expected to support field development, increase production and strengthen the country’s position as an attractive destination for oil and gas capital.

Policy certainty critical

Madam Hardcastle, however, stressed that sustaining the momentum would require Ghana to maintain an investment climate in which operators could make long-term decisions with confidence.

She identified a stable fiscal regime, transparent regulatory arrangements and efficient licensing processes as critical elements in maintaining investor confidence.

The resolution of the outstanding disputes, she suggested, therefore represents more than the settlement of individual disagreements between the government and industry players.

It provides a foundation for renewed cooperation between the State and petroleum companies at a time when Ghana is seeking to increase production, expand gas utilisation and attract fresh investment into its upstream industry.

With billions of dollars in new commitments now emerging, the challenge for the government and regulators will be to sustain the policy certainty that encouraged the investments while ensuring that petroleum resources deliver maximum value to the Ghanaian economy.

Ghana News.title: Land dispute turns deadly as man is allegedly stabbed with scissors at Achiase
Ghana News.content:
A land-related disagreement at Achiase, near Aboso in the Prestea Huni Valley Municipality of the Western Region, has ended in tragedy following the alleged stabbing death of a resident, Augustine Boah.

Boah is said to have sustained fatal injuries after he was allegedly attacked with a pair of scissors by a 24-year-old man, Kofi Yena, popularly known as “Pogba”.

The incident, which occurred on Thursday, August 20, 2026, has reportedly heightened tensions between the families of the two men, with the dispute believed to have been linked to a piece of land in the community.

According to accounts emerging from the area, the disagreement had been brewing for some time.

The latest confrontation was reportedly triggered by an earlier warning from Yena to the deceased’s son over the use of a route behind his family’s house with his tricycle.

The issue allegedly resurfaced on Thursday when Boah and Yena confronted each other, leading to a physical altercation.

During the confrontation, Yena is alleged to have used a pair of scissors to attack Boah, leaving him with injuries that subsequently proved fatal.

The circumstances surrounding the confrontation and what immediately preceded the alleged stabbing remain subject to police investigation.

Following the incident, Yena was arrested and taken into police custody as the police commenced investigations into the death.

Meanwhile, the body of Boah has been deposited at the morgue of the Tarkwa Municipal Hospital pending further procedures.

Ghana News.title: Muntaka orders police to crush vigilantism, unauthorised ‘self-defence’ groups
Ghana News.content:
The Minister for the Interior, Muntaka Mubarak, has directed the Ghana Police Service to intensify the fight against vigilantism and move swiftly to dismantle emerging groups being formed by individuals, political parties, traditional authorities and other organisations for self-protection.

He warned that the growing practice posed a threat to Ghana’s peace and security, particularly if such groups were allowed to operate outside the authority of the state.

Mr Muntaka gave the directive in Accra when he opened a regional commanders’ conference at the Ghana Police Headquarters, where he urged senior police officers to strengthen efforts to detect and deal with activities capable of undermining public order.

He said the formation of private forces for the protection of individuals or groups was prohibited under the Vigilantism and Related Offences Act, 2019 (Act 999), and should not be allowed to take root.

“We observe with concern a new trend of chiefs, political parties, individuals, and some organisations building forces for self-protection. The Vigilantism and Related Offences Act 2019 Act 999 is clear on this matter.

“These are illegal and should not be tolerated. There should be no forces for protection of any person or group except those authorised by the state. I therefore charge you and your commanders to nip this in the bud and bring perpetrators to book,” he said.

The Interior Minister said the Ghana Police Service had a critical responsibility to ensure that no parallel security structures emerged to challenge the authority of the state.

He, therefore, urged regional commanders to remain alert to signs of vigilantism and take decisive action against persons or organisations seeking to establish unauthorised security forces.

The directive comes amid concerns over the formation of groups ostensibly intended to provide security or protection for particular individuals, political interests or communities.

Mr Muntaka stressed that the state must remain the sole authority responsible for the legitimate use of force and the protection of citizens.

The Minister also expressed concern about the increasing circulation on social media of videos and other materials showing recruits undergoing training at security service institutions.

He directed commanders of the various security services to immediately strengthen controls to prevent the unauthorised recording and dissemination of such material.

“I am equally concerned about the growing number of officers and trainers in our training schools, allowing videos and other content of recruits undergoing training to be recorded and shared on social media. This practice must stop.

“I therefore direct all service commanders to ensure that appropriate controls are put in place to prevent the unauthorised recording, publication and circulation of images or videos of recruits in training,” he stated.

He said protecting information relating to the training of security personnel was important to maintaining the integrity and effectiveness of the country's security institutions.

The directive places greater responsibility on commanders and trainers to ensure that security training facilities are not used as sources of unauthorised social media content.

Mr Muntaka's two-pronged directive — against vigilantism and the unauthorised sharing of security training content — underscores the government's emphasis on strengthening state control over security operations and protecting the professionalism of Ghana's security services.
