World.title: Dangote to sell 30% shareholding of new refinery to East African countries – Report
World.content:
Dangote Group, the empire of Africa’s richest man Aliko Dangote, has offered a 30 per cent holding in its proposed 700,000 barrel-per-day (bpd) refinery to nations in East Africa, the region where the mega crude-processing plant is to be located, Bloomberg reported Friday.

Kenya, where the new refinery will be sited at the southeastern coastal town of Lamu, will take a 10 per cent stake estimated at around half a trillion dollars, David Ndii, a top economic adviser of President Ruto, told Bloomberg.

“The total for the region is about $1.5 billion. I don’t actually see a challenge in doing that, and if some of them are not off-taking we will backstop,” Mr Ndii was quoted as saying at a capital market conference in Nairobi on Thursday.

Ethiopia and Rwanda are said to have indicated willingness to participate.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Dangote is turning to business-friendly Kenya and other promising markets in East Africa to expand his multi-billion dollar empire after facing an avalanche of resistance from his home country Nigeria in bringing a refinery of similar capacity to completion.

The Nigerian refinery, situated in the outskirts of Lagos and initially projected to be completed in 2016, did not see the light of the day until eight years after, held back by logistic delay, infrastructure constraints and COVID-19 lockdowns.

The magnate, who has built his fortune around cement, sugar and a couple of fast-moving consumer products, accused international oil companies of sabotaging efforts at getting the refinery running seamlessly in its early days.

He claimed that the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority, which serves as the top watchdog for the midstream and downstream segments of the oil industry, issued new licences to some players to import “dirty fuel” as part of a broader conspiracy to frustrate his push to wean Nigeria off its longstanding dependency on fuel imports.

In the heat of the crisis, Farouk Ahmed, the CEO of the regulator at the time, resigned his appointment, while Mele Kyari, the immediate past managing director of state oil company NNPC Limited, whom Mr Dangote accused of surreptitiously running a fuel blending plant off the coast of Malta, was shown the exit door.

“I knew there would be a fight. But I didn’t know that the mafia in oil, they are stronger than the mafia in drugs,” he told an investment conference in June 2024.

A private placement, which raised $2.5 billion ahead of the Nigerian refinery’s planned $5 billion initial public offer scheduled for October, valued the refinery at $40 billion.

The private equity capital raise was 3.7 times, drawing interest from African institutional investors and institutional investors from outside the continent.

The groundbreaking of the Kenyan refinery is expected to kick off next month.

That puts the company on course to achieve the ambition of doubling its refining capacity to 1.4 million bpd in the next three years, with processing capacity at the refinery in Lagos already upped to 700,000 bpd from its original 650,000 bpd.

The planned refinery in Kenya is expected to cost $15 billion to $17 billion.

World.title: Tinubu suspends three permanent secretaries over fresh fake agency, orders alleged promoter’s arrest
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu has ordered the suspension of three permanent secretaries over the discovery of a new fake agency.

The phoney agency, known as the National Brands Development and Made in Nigeria Special Project Office, was said to be operating within the Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation.

The suspected permanent secretaries are M.S. Danjuma, Nadungu Gagare, and Richard P. Pheelangwah.

The president also ordered the immediate arrest of the alleged promoter of the fake agency, George Buchi Nwabueze.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The chairman of the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC), Musa Aliyu, who disclosed the developments to State House correspondents on Friday, said Mr Nwabueze “was discovered to also operate under four other variations of names.”

The four other name variations are “George Nathan, George Nathan Nwabueze, Hon. George Buchi Nwabueze, Prince Geroge Buchi Nwabueze and George Nwabueze.”

“I have briefed Mr President comprehensively on these new developments. ICPC will continue with its investigations,” the ICPC chairman said.

The discovery of the new fake agency was an offshoot of ICPC’s investigations into the alleged fictitious Presidential Foreign Investment Promotion Council (PFIPC).

The ICPC chair had disclosed after briefing President Tinubu on 6 August on the commission’s interim report that the probe discovered two additional fake agencies.

Mr Aliyu said he submitted the interim report on 6 August, exactly 30 days after the President ordered a probe into the matter.

Mr Aliyu said the commission recommended the prosecution of the self proclaimed Director-General of the organisation, Adeniyi Adeyemi, over alleged forgery, impersonation and related offences.

World.title: Kwara senator picks PDP ticket hours after quitting APC
World.content:
Senator Saliu Mustapha of the Kwara Central District has picked the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) ticket for the district, hours after resigning from the All Progressives Congress (APC).

Mustapha received the PDP senatorial ticket on Friday from the party’s Kwara State Chairman, Issa Bawa, formally making him the party’s candidate for the Kwara Central senatorial election in 2027.

The development follows his resignation from the APC amid a prolonged crisis within the ruling party in Kwara State.

Mustapha had run for the APC governorship ticket. Still, the party decided to give the ticket to the state’s northern senatorial district, eventually nominating the state House of Assembly speaker, Yakubu Danladi-Salihu.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The ruling party also nominated Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq as its senatorial candidate for the central district.

Mustapha announced his resignation on Thursday through statements shared on his verified social media handles.

In his resignation letter dated 14 August and addressed to the APC Ward Chairman of Gambari Ward 1 in Ilorin East Local Government Area, the senator said recent developments within the party, particularly under its leadership in Kwara, had eroded his confidence in the APC.

He said his decision followed weeks of consultations with his supporters, constituents and political stakeholders across the state.

Mustapha leaves APC

Mustapha said he joined the APC as a founding member because of his commitment to good governance, unity, and service to the people.

He, however, said the party’s leadership in Kwara had departed from the principles of unity and internal democracy on which the APC was founded.

“I believe political leadership must be anchored on integrity, competence, accountability, and a sincere commitment to the collective interest of the people,” he said.

“The current leadership of the party in Kwara State has fallen short of these standards, and this has eroded my confidence.”

The senator also assured his supporters that leaving the APC would not affect his commitment to Kwara Central and the state.

“To my constituents, supporters, political associates and stakeholders in Kwara State and beyond, I assure you that while my political platform may change, my principles, purpose, and commitment to the people remain unchanged,” he said.

His resignation came after months of disagreement between him and other aggrieved APC stakeholders, as well as the party’s leadership in the state.

From APC’s crisis to PDP’s

PREMIUM TIMES had earlier reported the growing tension within the Kwara APC following the party’s governorship primary and the subsequent controversy over its National Assembly candidates.

Mustapha was among the prominent aspirants who contested the APC governorship ticket but lost to Danladi-Salihu.

Governor AbdulRazaq is the APC candidate for the Kwara Central Senatorial District.

The developments fuelled speculation about Mustapha’s next political move.

He was also part of the G15 coalition of aggrieved APC stakeholders, which rejected the outcome of the party’s primary and demanded intervention from President Bola Tinubu and the APC national leadership.

Members of the group, including Mustapha, Deputy Senate Leader Lola Ashiru and Senator Ibrahim Oloriegbe, had publicly criticised the process through which the party’s candidates emerged.

At one of the protests in Ilorin, Mustapha called on President Tinubu to intervene.

“We are protesting because we are not happy with the way the party’s leadership handled the process that produced the candidates. We are not against anyone, but the process lacked fairness and inclusiveness,” he said.

The group had also warned that the internal crisis could undermine APC’s chances in the 2027 elections.

Defection was expected

The senator’s move to the PDP did not come as a surprise.

PREMIUM TIMES had previously reported the widening political options available to Mustapha and other members of the G15 as efforts to resolve the APC dispute appeared increasingly uncertain.

The PDP had also emerged as a possible platform for the senator to continue his political career after losing the APC governorship ticket and facing uncertainty about his senatorial seat.

The PDP’s decision to hand him its Kwara Central ticket now confirms those earlier political calculations.

His emergence also ends speculations over who would fly the PDP flag in the district.

The party had previously been linked with other possible candidates for the seat as political negotiations continued.

Fresh contest

Mustapha’s emergence sets up a direct contest with Gov AbdulRazaq, who is seeking the Kwara Central Senate seat on the APC platform after completing his second term as governor.

The contest is likely to attract significant attention because both men are prominent figures in Kwara politics and have previously operated within the same political platform.

Mustapha was elected to the Senate in 2023 on the APC platform.

ALSO READ: Kwara senator Saliu Mustapha resigns from APC

His departure means that he will now challenge the party under which he currently holds the seat.

The development could also reshape the broader political landscape ahead of the 2027 elections, particularly in Kwara Central and among members of the G15.

Wider implications

The senator’s defection comes at a critical point for the APC, which has been attempting to contain the fallout from its primaries.

The party’s governorship candidate, Danladi-Salihu, has acknowledged the grievances and said a reconciliation committee had been established to address them.

The APC leadership has maintained that its candidates emerged from primaries conducted in line with the party’s guidelines.

The Emir of Ilorin, Ibrahim Sulu-Gambari, has also publicly endorsed the APC candidates, praising AbdulRazaq’s administration and praying for their success.

Mustapha’s departure, however, means that APC’s reconciliation efforts now face a more difficult test.

His move to the PDP could also encourage further realignment among politicians and party members who were dissatisfied with the outcome of the APC primaries.

For the 2027 Kwara Central senatorial contest, the immediate consequence is clear. Mustapha will seek another term in the Senate under the PDP, while AbdulRazaq will attempt to secure the seat for the APC.

The contest is therefore likely to become one of the closely watched political battles in Kwara ahead of the 2027 general elections.

World.title: Deepening Public Procurement Reform: How BPP and perm secs are resetting governance, By Ismail Omipidan
World.content:
Change is inevitable. But implementing it always meets resistance from within and outside. Since assuming office about two years ago, the Director-General of the Bureau of Public Procurement (BPP), Dr Adebowale Adedokun, FCIPS, has faced that resistance head-on with a reform agenda aimed at transforming Nigeria’s procurement ecosystem.

He came in at a time when confidence in the Bureau was low. It was gathered that before his appointment, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu had considered shutting down the BPP, noting that it had “outlived its usefulness.” The period leading to 2023 was widely described as an era of “anything goes” at the Bureau.

This was captured by former BPP DG, Dr Emeka Eze, at the inaugural edition of “The Procurement Evolution” in June this year. Dr Eze, now Chairman of the FCT Civil Service Commission and pioneer DG of BPP from 2007 to February 2016, said he was the subject of numerous petitions during his tenure for blocking improper benefits from the procurement system.

“For nine years that I was DG, there were petitions flying everywhere. Fireworks everywhere. But after I left, for another eight years, no petitions, no fireworks,” Dr Eze said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He added: “The moment the current DG (Dr Adedokun) resumed, I noticed the fireworks and petitions have resumed again. It means there is something we are doing right which some people do not want. After I left office, I met one of those behind the petitions and asked why he had gone quiet. He said, ‘You blocked us from chopping.’”

Like every reformer, Dr Adedokun knows the journey demands courage, consistency, and collective resolve. Undeterred by naysayers, he has pressed ahead with reforms, backed by President Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda.

Re-engaging Permanent Secretaries

To align Ministries, Departments and Agencies (MDAs) with the reforms, the BPP revived the Permanent Secretaries’ Retreat after a four-year break.

The 2026 edition, themed “Strengthening Procurement Leadership and Accountability for Effective Budget Execution and National Development,” held from Thursday, July 9 to Sunday, 12 July 2026, at Four Points by Sheraton, Ikot Ekpene, Akwa Ibom State, was declared open by Vice President Kashim Shettima.

Addressing participants, Dr Adedokun described public procurement as “one of the most powerful instruments of governance” and “the bridge between budget approval and service delivery.”

He disclosed that BPP has initiated 23 key reforms to align Nigeria’s system with global best practices. These include: Proposed amendment of the Public Procurement Act, 2007, Development of a National Procurement Strategy Framework, Revised procurement thresholds, Community-based procurement, Contractor classification and categorisation, Full rollout of Electronic Government Procurement (e-GP), and the Nigeria First Policy among others.

He also announced that BPP helped the Federal Government save about ₦1.1 trillion in 2025 through improved price intelligence and budget evaluation, with weekly savings averaging ₦8 billion since January 2026.

“Roads are constructed through procurement. Hospitals are equipped through procurement. Schools are built through procurement. Therefore, the quality of procurement determines the quality of governance,” he said.

Stressing that Permanent Secretaries, as Accounting Officers, bear ultimate responsibility for compliance with the Act, Dr Adedokun said BPP has introduced administrative sanctions for erring procurement officers and a Debarment Policy to blacklist contractors who violate due process.

He urged MDAs to publish contract awards on their websites and the BPP portal, and to comply with circulars on budget implementation, contract variations, and agreements.

Dr Adedokun added that Nigeria’s reforms are gaining global recognition, citing the Sustainable Procurement, Environmental and Social Standards Enhancement Project (SPESSE) as an evidence. Under SPESSE, specialised undergraduate degrees in Sustainable Procurement have been established in six universities: Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria; University of Lagos; University of Benin; Abubakar Tafawa Balewa University, Bauchi; Federal University of Technology, Owerri; and Joseph Sarwuan Tarka University, Makurdi.

“Development partners and multilateral institutions have acknowledged Nigeria’s strides in institutionalising transparency and accountability in public procurement under President Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda,” he said.

“A budget is a covenant with the people. But procurement leadership is how we keep the covenant. Countries are developed by spending rightly. Only an accountable procurement system can guarantee that,” the BPP DG, added.

What Leaders Said

Representing the Vice President, Prof Tunji Olaopa, Chairman of the Federal Civil Service Commission, said procurement is now “a strategic instrument for economic growth, a driver of industrial development, a tool for promoting local content, and a mechanism for ensuring value for money.”

“It is an instrument of public trust. When procurement works, government delivers. When it fails, development suffers. The task before us is not just to comply with procedures but to strengthen procurement leadership, because no procurement system can outgrow the leadership behind it, “ he told participants.

Representing President Tinubu, SGF Senator George Akume, through his SSA, Prof Bernard Babatunde, said effective budget implementation depends on disciplined financial management and a procurement system that delivers value.

He lauded BPP’s reforms under Dr Adedokun and assured the Bureau of the SGF’s full support, adding that anyone involved in procurement fraud would be prosecuted.

The Head of the Civil Service of the Federation, Mrs Didi Esther Walson-Jack, noted that procurement sits at the centre of governance.

“When procurement works well, Government delivers. When procurement is delayed, weak or poorly managed, citizens feel the consequences,” she said.

She urged Accounting Officers to insist on due process, value for money, and timely delivery, adding: “Creativity must never replace compliance, and innovation must never weaken accountability.”

The Takeaway

At the end of the retreat, which featured sessions on budget implementation, procurement planning, leadership, and institutional coordination, the consensus was clear: procurement must be seen as a strategic tool for economic growth, job creation, and national competitiveness.

* Omipidan, an author, journalist and media consultant writes from Abuja.

World.title: Why nearly half of Nigeria’s listed companies paid no dividends in three years
World.content:
At least 60 of about 136 listed companies on the Nigerian Exchange (NGX) haven’t paid dividends for at least three years in the five years from 2021 to 2025, PREMIUM TIMES has found.

That compares with 51 companies in the half-decade period to 2021, when the number of quoted stocks was 156 (including ETFs), as reviewed in a previous PREMIUM TIMES report.

A deep dive by PREMIUM TIMES showed that many Nigerian stocks don’t pay dividends for a variety of reasons, including strategic, regulatory, and policy-related factors.

Some companies’ choice not to offer dividends to shareholders is not necessarily a drawback, nor is it a regulatory breach that authorities should look out for to sanction non-compliant firms.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

No rule exists anywhere in the country that obligates companies to always pay dividends to equity investors.

Companies such as Austin Laz, Cadbury, Caverton, Chams, Chellarams, Daar Communications, Dangote Sugar, Critical Minerals Financing Corporation (formerly Deep Capital), Ellah Lakes, Nigerian Enamelware, Eterna, ETranzact, Eunisell, Fortis Global, FTN Cocoa, Golden Guinea Breweries, Unity Bank and Guinness didn’t pay dividends regularly as they had been held back by negative retained earnings for years.

So also did International Breweries, Japaul Gold, Juli, Livestock Feeds, Mutual Benefits, Morison Industries, Multi-Trex, Nigerian Breweries, NCR Nigeria, Neimeth, Nestle, NSL Tech, Oando, Omatek, Premier Paints, PZ Cussons, Royal Exchange, RT Briscoe, SCOA, Tantalisers, Thomas Wyatt, Union Dicon, Universal Insurance, UPDC, Veritas Kapital, Coronation Insurance.

African Alliance, Afromedia, Ekocorp, Pharma Deko and STACO Insurance have not issued their audited accounts since at least 2022. On that ground, they have been unable to announce dividends.

The rest of the pack – from Briclinks Africa, Champion Breweries, Honeywell Flour, Ronchess Global Resources and John Holt to underwriters like Lasaco Assurance, Prestige Assurance, Regency Alliance and Sovereign Trust Insurance – are taking the long view, preferring to plough back profits into their operations rather than constantly share dividends to stockholders.

Companies ideally pay dividends from retained earnings, which aggregate the profits they have amassed over time.

In this review, companies like Aradel Holdings, Transcorp Power, Haldane McCall, VFD Group, Mecure Industries, Legend Internet and Zichis Agro Allied Industries were exempted because they attained public company status from 2023 onwards and are therefore too new to be fairly assessed by the yardstick of consistent dividend history.

The list also doesn’t account for exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or new listings within that time range, which didn’t offer dividends for three years at a minimum.

Top roadblocks

That a significant number of Nigerian public companies didn’t distribute cash dividends to shareholders over the five years ending in 2025 doesn’t validate the likelihood that they don’t take dividend payments seriously.

Among the hindrances to the potential of Nigerian quoted companies to pay dividends, loss-making ranks at the top of the pile, corporate reports’ data show.

Only nine of the companies under review for not paying dividends at all or not doing so consistently from 2021 to 2025 reported profits throughout that period or for most of it.

They comprised Bricklinks Africa, Champion Breweries, Honeywell Flour Mills, John Holt, Lasaco Assurance, Prestige Assurance, Regency Alliance, Ronchess Global Resources and Sovereign Trust Insurance.

That little changed from what happened in the 5 years to 2021, when the number of those that didn’t pay dividends was 5.

Nigeria’s corporate law prohibits public firms from posting losses when paying dividends, on the view that they must prioritise recovery over shareholder reward by channelling their financial resources towards restoring operations to profitability before other considerations.

“A company may, in a general meeting, declare dividends in respect of any year or other period only on the recommendation of the directors. The company may, from time to time, pay to the members such interim dividends as appear to the directors to be justified by the profits of the company,” says Section 426, Subsections 1-2 of CAMA 2020, the corporate legal framework governing businesses in Nigeria

“Subject to the provisions of this Act, dividends are payable to the shareholders only out of the distributable profits of the company,” it states further.

The sweeping FX reforms President Bola Tinubu introduced on taking office, specifically the various naira devaluation rounds between June 2023 and February 2024, spurred colossal losses among import-dependent businesses and companies with foreign-currency exposures.

From telcos like MTN Nigeria to consumer goods manufacturers like Nigerian Breweries, Guinness, PZ Cussons, Nestle, and Cadbury, the implications were dire and radical, at times forcing multinationals like GSK and Procter & Gamble to close shop and desert the country.

The financial distress that resulted led to wide-scale losses across sectors outside financial services, turning retained earnings into red, in turn hurting companies’ capacity to pay dividends.

“Not until 2025 did we see that companies started to find their footing back, with the exchange rate now more stable, the monetary authority now having more legroom to be able to defend the naira,” Oyindamola Oyenuga, investment research analyst at Meristem Securities, told PREMIUM TIMES.

She holds the position that the fact that a company doesn’t pay dividends for a certain period is a case of having to understand why that is so, noting how consumer goods stocks like Unilever and also UACN were paying dividends before the FX crisis erupted, halting the trend.

“During that period, there were lots of sell-downs on consumer goods stocks; they were hard hit. Many investors took their profits. They sold off consumer goods stocks. But now, we are seeing that (dividend payment) return. Investors responded negatively to the fact that companies were not paying dividends, and that was largely anticipated,” she remarked.

Yet, macroeconomic limitations are not the only brick wall to companies’ dividend distribution plans. Regulation sometimes throws spanners in the works.

That played out in the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN)’s order to banks in June 2025, demanding that those with forbearance loans refrain from paying dividends until they purged their balance sheets of toxic assets.

Big banking institutions such as Access Holdings, First HoldCo, and United Bank for Africa, and mid-tier lender Fidelity Bank, finished the year without paying a dime to shareholders, breaking with a corporate tradition they had religiously maintained for years.

It was in light of this regulatory stringency and the frustration it provoked in shareholders expectant of a handsome payout for 2025 that Access Holdings chairman, Aigboje Aig-Imoukhuede, stepped in to calm nerves last month at the annual general meeting.

The banking group, Nigeria’s largest public company by assets, hit a revenue milestone of N5.5 trillion and scaled up total assets by almost a quarter to N51.6 trillion in the last financial year. Likewise, its pre-tax profit crossed the N1 trillion mark in the period, making it one of only three lenders to achieve that.

“Without a doubt, those results do not speak to an institution that cannot pay a dividend. Of course, we can pay a dividend,” Mr Aig-Imoukhuede told shareholders in reassurance.

“It therefore implies that we were restricted from sharing dividends with our shareholders for specific reasons,” he stated further.

One of those was the fact that the group was still carrying forbearance loans in its portfolio during the year.

That said, fresh complications have arisen beyond the constraint imposed by the urgency of compliance with forbearance loan rules on lenders willing to distribute dividends.

In the spirit of international best practices, the CBN is now asking that banks’ investment in subsidiaries be 10 per cent or less of shareholders’ funds.

Until lenders enforce the rule, dividend distribution is out of the question, the Nigerian banking industry top watchdog has said.

It is particularly compounding the ordeal of bank holdcos like Access Holdings, where aggressive expansion into verticals like payments, pensions and consumer lending has been at fever pitch in the last few years.

Corporate character factors

Across the globe, companies that are extremely passionate about growth, by nature, rarely focus on immediate shareholder value, which is largely anchored in regular cash distributions.

As part of their corporate philosophy, companies of this stripe are inclined to invest the bulk, if not all, of their profits back into their operations.

In this case, expansion is a top priority, and a readiness to wait for investment to deliver long-term returns is almost always a virtue that potential investors in such companies must imbibe.

That especially applies to technology companies, given that their operations are, by default, capital-intensive.

The pressure of growth requires them to commit a substantial outlay to developing key infrastructure and bringing their services and solutions up to speed with the latest trends and developments in a pretty dynamic, fast-paced industry, where consumers’ tastes and preferences change at the speed of light.

Against this backdrop, US tech titans like Amazon, Twitter, Netflix, and Tesla don’t pay dividends.

Companies running a residual dividend policy are typically growth-oriented, and tend to focus on capital expenditures and working capital needs more than paying dividends.

The orientation of these firms is that every available cash should be put to use, either to facilitate capital projects or for cash distribution rather than being held.

In this class is Access Holdings, which in recent years has used the lion’s share of its retained earnings to drive a formidable pan-African expansion, unmatched by any Nigerian company, and broadly branch out beyond its core banking business into other promising sectors within financial services.

Investors often see growth stocks as holding prospects of capital appreciation, which usually make up for the dividends they hardly pay.

To meet the listing needs of such companies, the NGX has set up a dedicated listing segment called the Growth Board, which admits companies with relatively small market capitalisation and promise for growth.

It is specially designed for technology firms and SMEs across different sectors of the economy.

On the face of it, growth stocks, judging by their price-to-earnings (PE) ratio, which is characteristically high, are expensive.

But that usually conceals the ultimate value of those stocks, which their current worth doesn’t reveal and which is the number one attraction of investors, whose orientation is towards growth rather than value.

PE ratio, a fundamental analysis metric, compares a company’s current share price with its earnings per share, indicating how much investors are paying for every dollar/naira of profit a company makes.

“I think I said at the last AGM, ‘shareholders who don’t have the time to wait for dividends, this is not the company for you,’” Chuka Mordi, the chief executive of Lagos-listed agro-processor Ellah Lakes, told CNBC Africa in February.

He was emphasising his company’s prioritisation of growth above everything else, its tenacity to pass over shareholder value for now to save up ample cash that is able to pivot the company through its current expansion phase and out of the perennial loss-making and a negative cash flow that have hammered operations for years.

Whether through dividend payment or capital appreciation or both ways, a stock must have a means of compensating investment for people to find it worth investing in.

“If a company “takes up a strategy that they want to expand, for example Access Bank or you see that UACN is expanding and they’ve acquired CHI, that gives the prospect that this company is expanding their operations and are going to get bigger or they’ll have a wider reach in the market,” Ms Oyenuga said in response to whether stocks that don’t pay dividends stand a chance of capital appreciation.

According to her, the products of such companies will ultimately enlarge and, for that reason, it is going to trickle down to sales and eventually profitability.

Investors leverage such updates within the company or the growth plans the company is pursuing, she noted, which are usually priced in when buying the stock.

“Certain policies could be taken, certain directions could be taken by management or certain strategies could be put in place in order to facilitate growth. Investors respond to that, and it could drive capital appreciation,” she added.

World.title: The Osogbo Test: The election that put INEC on trial, by Stephanie Shaakaa
World.content:
File: INEC chairman Joash Amupitan

By Sunday morning, Osogbo had begun to look like a city coming out of a long night.

Campaign posters still clung to walls. Election notices hung where they had been pasted. Roads that had carried convoys, party agents and anxious voters were returning to ordinary traffic. Somewhere, tired election officials were heading home after a night that had stretched beyond the closing of the polls.

But beneath the celebration and disappointment was a quieter question:

Can Nigerians still believe an election when it is over?

That question is bigger than Ademola Adeleke. It is bigger than Bola Oyebamiji. Ultimately, it is bigger than Osun.

Adeleke won the August 15 governorship election with 511,067 votes against Oyebamiji’s 444,815, securing another term. The returning officer announced the result and the certificate of return followed.

But Nigerian elections are no longer judged by arithmetic alone.

There is now a second election after the first one has ended. It is fought in the minds of citizens, on television, across social media and in conversations that continue long after the ballot boxes are packed away.

It is the election over whether the result deserves to be believed.

That was the election INEC walked into.

Osun was never simply another off cycle contest. It carried the memory of every Nigerian election that had left citizens suspicious or unconvinced. It carried the promises made about BVAS and electronic transmission. It carried the lessons of previous logistical failures and, above all, the enormous burden of public distrust.

INEC was not being asked merely to conduct an election. It was being asked to demonstrate that the institution entrusted with conducting Nigerian elections could still be trusted with one.

That is a much higher standard.

For years, Nigeria has discussed electoral reform as though the problem were principally mechanical. How do we identify voters? How do we prevent multiple accreditation? How quickly can results be transmitted? How do we improve logistics? How can technology reduce human interference?

Those questions matter. But Osun exposed the question beneath them:

What happens when technology improves faster than public trust?

We have fallen into a dangerous illusion: believing that hardware can cure a software problem. You can deploy sophisticated biometric accreditation and faster transmission systems, but they cannot outrun bad faith. A machine can authenticate a voter. It cannot stop a desperate political class from treating the collation centre as a theatre of war.

Technology can improve the mechanics of voting. It cannot reform the culture of survival surrounding Nigerian politics.

This is the problem INEC now faces. It is no longer fighting only logistical problems.

It is fighting memory.

Every delayed material carries the memory of a previous delay. Every unexplained interruption invites comparison with an earlier controversy. Every result that takes longer than expected to appear creates space for rumours to move faster than official information.

In modern Nigeria, silence is rarely empty.

Somebody fills it.

That somebody may be a party agent, a commentator, a political operative or an ordinary voter watching results unfold on a phone. By the time an official explanation arrives, suspicion may already have travelled halfway across the country.

This is why transparency cannot mean merely releasing information eventually. It means communicating while the process is happening.

Osun offered evidence that INEC can manage a fiercely contested election without the entire electoral machine breaking down. Across the state’s 3,763 polling units, there were delays and logistical pressures, but the machinery held.

That matters.

Nigerian elections have sometimes been defined by the moment when the machinery stops holding. A delay becomes confusion. Confusion becomes suspicion. Suspicion becomes confrontation.

Osun did not descend into that kind of systemic breakdown.

That is a credit to the commission.

But it is also where the praise should become careful.

INEC should not mistake a successful election for a completed reform project. Osun was a test, not a graduation.

The broader question of credibility remains open because technology can improve mechanics without repairing the culture surrounding an election.

There is another uncomfortable feature of Nigerian elections: the security presence.

Security is necessary. Voters have a right to protection. Election officials have a right to safety.

But there is something troubling about a democracy that increasingly needs the visible force of the security state to reassure citizens that they are safe enough to exercise political freedom.

The security personnel may protect the ballot, but their very presence is an indictment. It is a physical monument to mutual hostility, a reminder that we have built a political system so dangerous that casting a vote can require a garrison.

Nigeria cannot permanently secure democracy by surrounding every election with the atmosphere of a military operation. At some point, the political culture itself has to become less lethal.

That responsibility does not belong to INEC alone.

It belongs to the political class.

Politicians have helped turn elections into existential battles. Too much money is invested in winning. Too much political survival is attached to office. Losing can therefore feel less like losing a contest and more like losing everything.

That is how democracy becomes warfare by other means.

And once politics becomes war, every institution becomes a battlefield.

INEC becomes an enemy to one side and an ally to the other. Security agencies become objects of suspicion. Results become weapons. Technology becomes either proof of progress or evidence of conspiracy, depending on whose candidate is winning.

No electoral commission can permanently survive that culture without being dragged into it. INEC can administer the contest. It cannot cure the desperation surrounding the contest.

That is why the ultimate verdict on Osun should not be whether INEC deserves applause or condemnation. The more important question is whether the election moved Nigeria closer to something we have discussed for decades but rarely achieved consistently.

An election whose winner does not require everyone else to believe they were cheated.

That is the real test.

A credible democracy does not require universal agreement. The loser does not have to love the result. Supporters do not have to celebrate the opposing candidate.

But there must be a point at which a citizen can say, with disappointment but without despair:

My candidate lost, but the process was legitimate. That sentence is the foundation of democratic stability.

Without it, every election becomes a prelude to the next crisis. With it, democracy becomes something more durable than the temporary triumph of one political party.

This is why Osun matters beyond the numbers. Adeleke’s strength in Ede North, Ede South and Osogbo mattered politically. Oyebamiji’s performance in places such as Irewole and Ilesa East mattered politically. The final margin mattered politically.

But the greater significance lies in what happened between those numbers.

Did voters get the opportunity to vote? Did officials perform their duties? Did technology work sufficiently to support transparency? Were problems contained rather than allowed to overwhelm the process? Were results generated through a chain citizens could follow?

And when the winner was announced, did the country have enough confidence in the process to accept that announcement as legitimate?

Those questions will outlive the campaign posters and the politicians.

Nigeria is heading toward elections in which the stakes will be higher than they were in Osun. Lessons from off cycle elections eventually travel to the national stage.

That makes Osogbo important.

It gives INEC an opportunity to learn before the stakes become even larger.

The lesson should not be that technology has solved Nigerian elections. It has not.

Technology is useful only when surrounded by competent administration, transparent communication, institutional independence and political restraint. The ballot is not protected by a machine alone. It is protected by the integrity of the people operating it.

And that brings us back to the question with which Osun leaves the country.

Can Nigerians still believe an election when it is over?

The honest answer is that belief cannot be demanded.

It has to be earned.

Not with speeches, press conferences or declarations that an election was free and fair.

It is earned slowly, polling unit by polling unit, election by election, through thousands of ordinary decisions that tell citizens the system is working as it should.

Trust is built in small moments. It is destroyed in small moments too.

That is why Osun should not be remembered simply as the election that returned Ademola Adeleke to the Osun State Government House.

It should be remembered as an election in which INEC itself was being tested.

Not tested on whether it could produce a winner. That is the easy part.

The harder test was whether it could produce enough confidence in the process that Nigerians could live with the winner.

Because a democracy does not collapse all at once. It erodes quietly, one lost election at a time, until citizens look at a ballot box and see nothing left inside it.

That is the standard Osogbo has placed before INEC.

The real result of the Osun election cannot be found only in 511,067 votes or 444,815 votes.

It is found in something far more fragile.

Whether Nigerians can still look at a ballot box and believe there is something inside it worth trusting.

World.title: How Federal might came to Osun and met the people, by Stephanie Shaakaa
World.content:
File: Governor Ademola Adeleke

Osun was supposed to be a governorship election.

Then Abuja arrived.

The problem is not that Abuja came to Osun. The problem is what Nigerian democracy becomes when Abuja can become the largest political presence in a state election.

What followed was not illegal simply because it was powerful. Political parties are entitled to mobilise. Governors are entitled to campaign for their party. National leaders can travel to states and ask voters to support their candidates. There is nothing inherently undemocratic about any of that.

The discomfort begins somewhere else.

It begins when a state election starts to look like a national political operation, when the machinery of a ruling party becomes so enormous that the distinction between party strength and the aura of government power begins to blur.

That is what made Osun worth watching.

The All Progressives Congress did not treat the August 15 election as an ordinary contest. It constituted a national campaign council that was initially announced as 276 members and later reported at 291, drawing in governors, National Assembly leaders, ministers, federal and state lawmakers and senior party figures from across the country. Imo Governor Hope Uzodimma was made chairman, with Yobe Governor Mai Mala Buni, Senate President Godswill Akpabio and Speaker Tajudeen Abbas among the senior figures in the leadership of the campaign structure.

Then, as the campaign entered its final hours, the spectacle became even more visible. Four serving governors were reported in Osogbo for the APC’s final mega rally .Uzodimma, Edo’s Monday Okpebholo, Kogi’s Ahmed Usman Ododo and Ondo’s Lucky Aiyedatiwa. They were joined by Akpabio and other national political heavyweights.

There was nothing subtle about the message.

Abuja was interested in Osun.

The APC itself had already described the election as a “must win” contest and as a crucial test of its readiness for 2027. Its national chairman said the party would deploy its nationwide political structures, elected officials and grassroots network to reclaim the state.

Again, none of this, by itself, proves that federal government resources were unlawfully used for partisan purposes. That would require evidence, and serious political writing should not manufacture it.

But democracy is concerned with more than illegality.

It is also concerned with power.

And power has a psychological dimension.

When a candidate goes into a state election surrounded by governors, ministers, senators, the leadership of the National Assembly and the full political machinery of the party controlling the federal government, voters do not see only a campaign team. They see the weight of the centre.

That weight is often deliberately amplified to manufacture an air of inevitability. The concentration of national heavyweights in a state capital is frequently deployed as a psychological tool,a bandwagon effect designed to demoralize local opposition, overwhelm undecided voters, and signal that resistance is futile.

That weight can be felt without anyone issuing a threat.

It can be communicated in a sentence as ordinary as the one APC National Secretary Ajibola Basiru delivered during the campaign, when he urged Osun voters to choose an APC governor because, he argued, the state would benefit from having a governor whose party controls the Federal Government.

There is a legitimate argument inside that proposition. Federal and state governments work together. A governor who belongs to the governing party may indeed find cooperation with Abuja easier.

But there is another question hiding inside it.

When does cooperation become leverage?

And what happens to federalism when voters begin to hear a state election partly as a choice between having access to Abuja and being outside the governing party at the centre?

That is not a trivial question.

A governorship election is supposed to answer a relatively simple question. Who do the people of this state want to govern them?

It should not quietly become another question.Who will give us the best relationship with the President?

Those questions are not the same.

One is about representation.

The other is about political dependency.

This is the deeper danger of federal might in state elections. It does not necessarily arrive carrying a threat. Sometimes it arrives carrying promises, access, prestige and proximity to power. It tells voters that the road to development may be smoother if they choose the candidate who sits on the same political side as Abuja.

Yet, when external actors descend too heavily, they frequently miscalculate the local psyche. Electorates often view an overwhelming federal onslaught not as a persuasive pitch, but as an infringement on their political maturity,a subtle insult that triggers a protective local backlash and turns the ballot box into a referendum on local pride versus external dictation.

Perhaps that is still viewed as legitimate political persuasion by its architects.

But we should still ask what kind of democracy we are building when the federal government becomes such a powerful presence in contests that are supposed to be decided at the state level.

Nigeria is a federation, not a political pyramid in which every important decision must eventually be traced back to the centre.

A governor should be able to govern effectively without owing his legitimacy to the President. A state should be able to choose an opposition governor without being made to feel that it has chosen political isolation.

Anything else risks turning federalism into patronage.

And that is where the Osun election becomes particularly instructive.

Because after all the governors came, after the national leaders mobilised, after the ruling party assembled one of the most formidable campaign structures imaginable, the voters still had the last word.

Ademola Adeleke won with 511,067 votes against Bola Oyebamiji’s 444,815, carrying 19 of the state’s 30 local government areas.

The national political machine had arrived.

The electorate did not surrender its independence.

That is perhaps the most important lesson of Osun.

Power can campaign.

It cannot vote.

Governors can stand on platforms and make promises. Ministers can explain the advantages of alignment with Abuja. Party chairmen can assemble structures that stretch across the country. National lawmakers can descend on a state and transform a local rally into a national spectacle.

But when the curtain closes and the voter enters the polling booth, all of that power must become irrelevant for a few precious seconds.

The voter stands alone with the ballot.

That small privacy is one of democracy’s greatest protections.

It is also why politicians should be careful about becoming intoxicated by the size of their own machinery.

The APC’s campaign in Osun demonstrated impressive organisation. There is nothing wrong with a political party knowing how to mobilise. In fact, weak political parties are a danger to democracy too.

But there is a difference between political organisation and political omnipotence.

The first strengthens democracy.

The second begins to frighten it.

This distinction matters particularly as Nigeria approaches 2027. When ruling parties treat off-cycle state contests as militarized proxy tests of national supremacy, they exhaust public goodwill, strain state resources, and turn routine democratic transitions into high-stakes existential battles.

If the lesson political parties take from Osun is that every state election should become a test of the federal government’s strength, then state politics will gradually become an extension of presidential politics. Governors will increasingly be judged not by what they can do for their people but by how close they are to the centre. Opposition parties will be forced to campaign not only against candidates but against the gravitational pull of Abuja itself.

That would be a terrible direction for a federation.

And the principle should apply regardless of who occupies Aso Rock.

Today the APC controls the Federal Government and has the machinery to deploy its national political establishment into a state contest. Tomorrow another party may control Abuja and do exactly the same thing.

The objection, therefore, should not be partisan.

It should be constitutional in spirit and democratic in principle.

No president should need to fear an opposition governor. No state should need to belong to the President’s party before it can expect fair treatment. And no voter should ever be made to feel that choosing the “wrong” party means choosing development’s wrong side.

That is not federalism.

That is political dependence.

Osun has given Nigeria an unusually useful warning because the people of the state ultimately demonstrated that the centre can come with all its weight and still fail to determine the outcome.

The APC brought governors.

The people brought ballots.

The APC brought national structures.

The people brought their judgment.

The APC brought Abuja’s political gravity.

The people remained in Osun.

And that is the point Nigerian democracy must never forget.

A political party can bring the whole country to a state election, but it cannot bring the whole country into the polling booth.

There, for one brief moment, the governor, the minister, the senator, the party chairman and the President disappear.

There is only the voter and the ballot.

That is where federal might must end.

Because the moment Abuja becomes the invisible candidate in a state election, the election is no longer simply about who should govern the state.

It becomes a test of whether the people still believe that the state belongs to them.

Osun answered that question more clearly than the politicians expected.

Abuja came calling.

The people answered at the ballot box.

Vanguard News

World.title: The meat we eat and the years we lose: How Nigeria’s abattoirs quietly erode our life expectancy
World.content:
By Dr. Gani Enahoro

Nigeria is a country of paradoxes. We boast one of Africa’s largest populations, a youthful demographic, and a livestock sector that is valued at an estimated ₦30 trillion.

Yet, we also carry the grim badge of having the lowest life expectancy in the world, a mere 55 years from an average of 73.8, according to the United Nations World Population Prospects (2026). It is a statistic so jarring that it forces us to confront uncomfortable truths about how Nigerians live, suffer, and die.

We often attribute our low life expectancy to malaria, childbirth complications, infectious diseases, insecurity, and the psychological trauma of banditry and kidnapping. But buried beneath these headline causes is a quieter, more pervasive threat, the food we eat, especially the meat that forms a central part of our diet. Unknown to many, a lot of people die from food poisoning traceable to meat sources, or in some cases had contracted viral or bacterial diseases through wrong processing of meat and its byproducts. This is not an exaggeration. It is a national emergency hiding in plain sight.

The hidden link between food safety and life expectancy

Life expectancy is not only shaped by dramatic events like insurgency or epidemics. It is also shaped by the slow, daily accumulation of risks, particularly in poor nutrition, contaminated food, chronic exposure to pathogens, and preventable illnesses that chip away at health over time. Nigeria’s abattoirs, unfortunately, sit at the heart of this problem. Across the country, abattoirs are legally under the control of local governments, which in theory, should ensure community-level easy oversight. However, in reality, it has produced a system where weak structures, poor funding, and a lack of veterinary supervision have turned many slaughterhouses into public health hazards.

The consequences are dire and far-reaching, as meat enters the food chain without proper ante-mortem and post-mortem inspection. Diseased or even pregnant animals are slaughtered and sold without restraint. Butchers often gang up and resist veterinary directives, relying instead on dangerous traditional practices. I am a veterinarian, trained at the University of Ibadan in the eighties. During an ambulatory rotation, at Bodija abattoir, a butcher sliced through a raised tuberculous lesion, and swallowed a piece in its raw form. His intention was not to commit suicide, it was directly to challenge our authority, although he paid dearly with illness as we later learned. That action, however, symbolized the deep cultural and systemic rot that endangers millions on a daily basis.

Hygiene and safety standards are abysmal in our abattoirs, with no care for personal protective equipment (PPE). There are open drains, where dungs are emptied, contaminated water, flies of different types, and unregulated waste disposal methods. All these are not helped by the weak government policies, such as public-private concessioning, which prioritizes revenue over safety.

The result, is that Nigerians across the board unknowingly consume meat contaminated with tuberculosis, brucellosis, salmonella, E. coli, parasites, and dangerous chemical residues. These illnesses may not always kill instantly, but they weaken the body, damage organs, and shorten lifespan.

The Livestock Sector: A giant calling for help

Nigeria is the largest livestock producer in West Africa. The National Bureau of Statistics estimates 54.81 million cattle, 64.93 million sheep and 138.95 million goats, 16 million pigs and 683.68 million poultry birds. These numbers reflect enormous economic potential, with a corresponding huge public health responsibility. Unfortunately, these animals are not managed intensively and in grazing reserves or ranches for necessary support and controls to optimize their yields for Nigeria. Instead, they are “naturalized wanderers” from other countries, moving freely across borders, contracting and transmitting diseases. With the suspension of FAO’s ECTAD support and limited national surveillance, Nigeria faces heightened vulnerability to trans-boundary animal diseases. When diseased animals end up in poorly regulated abattoirs, the danger multiplies.

Meat Processing: Where safety should begin But often ends

Veterinarians use the term wholesomeness to describe meat that is safe for consumption. Achieving wholesomeness requires processes that includes ante-mortem inspection, which is examining animals clinically before slaughter. This is followed by post-mortem inspection, examining organs and carcasses after slaughter. Then condemnation of diseased parts, by setting aside and removing unsafe meat from the food chain. A proper disposal method preventing environmental contamination ideally concludes the stages. In functional systems, these steps are non-negotiable, but in our country, they are optional at best with a lot of dragging and haggling.

Local governments lack veterinary personnel. In several states, veterinarians serving as area veterinary officers are made to cater for two or three local government areas. They are supported by an equally short supplied paraprofessionals. Where veterinarians exist at all and manage to visit the abattoirs, their other equally demanding responsibilities are abandoned. They disrespectfully face resistance from butchers who see inspection as interference and their presence as disturbance. Concessionaires also feel uncomfortable at their presence, seeing it as disruptive of normal flow of their activities, as they naturally prioritize profit over safety. Abattoir infrastructure across Nigeria is largely dilapidated, with unreliable water supply and chaotic waste disposal methods. The slaughter slabs are often open-air, competing for ownership with flies, exposed to dust, animals, and human traffic. This is not merely unhygienic, it is deadly.

The consequences of food poisoning, zoonotic infections, and chronic exposure to pathogens contribute to gastrointestinal diseases, liver and kidney damage, immune suppression, chronic inflammation, and eventually long-term organ failure. These conditions reduce healthy life expectancy and increase mortality, especially among children, pregnant women, and the elderly.

The economic cost of unsafe meat

Beyond health, Nigeria’s abattoir crisis has economic consequences. Countries that maintain strict food safety standards will not import meat from nations with poor slaughterhouse practices. I have warned at different fora and in previous articles, that the trade departments of foreign embassies, routinely gather intelligence on food safety in Nigeria. Their advisory is simple, Nigerian meat is unsafe. I have seen meat-filled coolers of different sizes crated in as diplomatic cargoes, by expatriates who had short job rotations in Nigeria. Some disguised the meat as being halal and the only type they eat, as a reason for such level of distrust in our meat. When things continue this way, it means lost export opportunities, and foreign exchange earnings, lost jobs in the livestock value chain and loss of credibility in international markets. After all, how will a rag-wearing man promise to gift new clothes to another?. A country that cannot guarantee safe meat for its citizens cannot convince the world to buy its products.

Why meat matters for life expectancy

Life expectancy is a composite measure, that reflects how people live, what they eat, the diseases they contract, and the healthcare they receive. It also considers the trauma they endure, and the environment they inhabit. Nigeria’s abattoirs contribute silently but significantly to this equation. Unsafe meat increases disease burden, which reduces productivity. A reduced productivity deepens poverty, which limits access to healthcare, and a limited healthcare increases mortality. It is a vicious cycle, and if Nigeria is serious about improving life expectancy, food safety must become a national priority, not a local government afterthought.

Way forward

To break this cycle, Nigeria must adopt a multi-level implementation strategy. This should include a revision of the legal framework, such that local governments cannot continue to bear sole responsibility for abattoirs. The states and the federal government must play stronger regulatory and supervisory roles.

Veterinarians must lead slaughterhouse operations, in order to professionalize abattoir management, while butchers should be trained and certified, not just in trade unionism. They should have basic knowledge of public health, biosecurity and biosafety measures. The conditions of concessioning abattoirs to contractors should prioritize safety, over and above revenue generation. Nigeria needs several hygienic slaughterhouses, with modern infrastructure, running water, waste treatment systems, cold chain facilities and disease surveillance units.

To strengthen animal health systems, Nigeria should internalize its trans-boundary disease control programs, without over-reliance on foreign funding from development partners. We should expand veterinary activities across the country. Governments should employ more veterinarians and paraprofessionals, and create more animal control posts to regulate movements in and out of our borders. Where employment embargoes exist, government could contract statutory veterinary services like meat inspection and disease surveillance to veterinary private practitioners. Cultural practices that endanger public health must be replaced with science-based knowledge, through a structured nationwide food safety education programme. Inter-ministerial collaborations, in the One-Health framework should integrate abattoir reforms into national health planning. Food safety should be part of Nigeria’s deliberate strategy to raise life expectancy.

In conclusion, lives can be saved through safer meat, and Nigeria’s life expectancy will not rise by accident. It will rise through deliberate reforms that address both dramatic and silent killers. Unsafe meat is one of those silent killers, ubiquitous, underestimated, and deadly. If we fix our abattoirs, we will save lives, strengthen our livestock economy, and restore public confidence in the food we eat. More importantly, we will give Nigerians a fighting chance to live longer, and healthier lives. The time to act is now. Unsafe meat is not just a food problem, it is a national life expectancy problem.

Dr Enahoro is former President, Nigerian Veterinary Medical Association

World.title: Autopsy ordered after man dies in Bauchi vigilante custody
World.content:
By Christopher Ameh, Bauchi

BAUCHI: Homicide detectives have launched an investigation into the death of a 39-year-old man, Abdulrazak Ibrahim, while in the custody of a local vigilante group in Bauchi metropolis.

The Bauchi State Police Command confirmed the incident on Friday, saying three members of the vigilante group had been arrested and detained in connection with the death.

According to preliminary police findings, Ibrahim was invited to the Bakin Kura Vigilante Office following a theft complaint lodged against him by his mother, Hauwa Ibrahim.

The community security group was reportedly tasked with investigating the allegation, recovering the stolen items and identifying possible buyers of the property.

However, Ibrahim died under unclear circumstances while being held at the facility.

The Chairman of the Bakin Kura Vigilante Group reported the incident to the police on Thursday, August 20, 2026, at about 6:39pm.

The Police Public Relations Officer, SP Nafiu Habib, said the command subsequently deployed homicide detectives from the ‘A’ Division Township to the scene.

He said three vigilante members were arrested for questioning, while Ibrahim’s body was deposited at the mortuary of the Abubakar Tafawa Balewa University (ATBU) Teaching Hospital, Bauchi.

According to him, preliminary examination of the body revealed no visible signs of physical violence or trauma.

He added that an autopsy would be conducted to determine the actual cause of death.

The Commissioner of Police, CP Sani-Omolori Aliyu, ordered a thorough investigation into the incident to ensure that justice was served.

The commissioner condemned extrajudicial actions and warned individuals and community security groups against resorting to jungle justice.

He urged members of the public to remain calm, assuring them that the outcome of the investigation would be made public.

World.title: Bauchi police launch major campaign to shield youth from political and digital thuggery
World.content:
By Christopher Ameh, Bauchi

The Bauchi State Police Command has officially launched a major security and youth inclusion campaign to combat the rising wave of political and digital thuggery among young people in the state.

The initiative was unveiled during a one-day dialogue held at the Police Officers’ Mess on Jos Road to mark the 26th edition of International Youth Day 2026. Organised in partnership with the National Youth Leadership and Security Initiative, the campaign runs under the theme: “My Future is Greater than Political and Digital Thuggery.”A Strategic Alliance for Peace.

The high-level event drew a diverse crowd of stakeholders, including members of the State Executive Council, representatives of the Emir of Bauchi, traditional rulers, and the Police Officers Wives Association (POWA). Civil society organisations, the Police Community Relations Committee (PCRC), academics, youth leaders, media practitioners, and the Joint Association of Persons with Disabilities were also in attendance to build a unified front for sustainable peace.

Opening the ceremony, the Bauchi State Commissioner of Police, CP Sani-Omolori Aliyu, emphasized that the command is heavily prioritizing community policing and youth inclusion to prevent crime.

He challenged the youth in attendance to reject the temptations of political manipulation and online thuggery, urging them instead to act as ambassadors for national development.

The campaign features a strategic hand-off to the Police Campaign Against Cultism and Other Vices (POCACOV) for grassroots execution. It also included an enlightenment drama and a keynote address by ACP Muhammad Musa Ahmadu, alongside goodwill messages from the Bauchi State Chief Security Adviser, the INEC Resident Electoral Commissioner, and the National Youth Council of Nigeria (NYCN).

A major highlight of the event was an open, moderated dialogue between police leadership and young participants.

The interactive session featured expert presentations on critical contemporary issues:Responsible Citizenship: Led by Prof. Bala Sulaiman Dalhat of Abubakar Tafawa Balewa University (ATBU). Security & Crime Prevention: Presented by DSP Muhammad A. Manga of the State Criminal Investigation Department (SCID). Building Public Trust: Detailed by Prof. Musa Adamu Wunti of Sa’adu Zungur University.Legal Risks of Thuggery: Outlined by the Acting State Legal Officer, DSP Barr. Kawu I. Mu’azu.

The command distributed copies of a book titled ‘ESTEEMED YOUTH’, which was personally donated to local youth groups by the Inspector General of Police, IGP Olatunji Rilwan Disu.

He expressed his gratitude to all partners and reiterated that empowering young people remains the single most effective strategy for securing the state’s future.

World.title: Abiodun receives hundreds of PDP, ADC defectors into APC, mobilises Ogun East for 2027
World.content:
*Says opposition has nothing to campaign with, set to flag off Ago-Iwoye–Ibadan road Monday

Ogun State Governor and leader of the All Progressives Congress (APC), Prince Dapo Abiodun, on Friday formally welcomed hundreds of former members of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and African Democratic Congress (ADC), including party leaders across the nine local government areas of Ogun East Senatorial District, into the ruling APC.

The defectors were received at an elaborate reception held at the Ojude-Oba carnival ground in Ijebu-Ode, which was filled to capacity with APC members, supporters and the new entrants.

Welcoming the defectors, Governor Abiodun described their decision to join the APC as a demonstration that they had “seen the light”, assuring them of equal treatment and full integration into the party.

“We are happy you have seen the light and you have decided to follow the light. You have become one of us from now on,” he said.

The governor urged the new and existing members to return to their respective wards and mobilise support for the APC ahead of the 2027 general elections, expressing confidence that the party would retain its dominance in the state.

Abiodun said the achievements of his administration since 2019 had distinguished the APC from opposition parties, particularly in the area of infrastructure, noting that more than 100 roads had been constructed across Ogun East, including about 26 roads in Ijebu-Ode alone.

He listed some of the ongoing and completed projects in the senatorial district to include the Gateway International Airport, major road projects, the Olokola Deep Sea Port, the Olokola-Kajola Gas Industrial Free Zone, oil exploration in Ogun Waterside and other economic infrastructure.

The governor also announced that the reconstruction of the Ago-Iwoye–Ibadan Road would be flagged off on Monday alongside the Minister of Works, Senator Dave Umahi.

According to him, the road runs from Ijebu-Ode through Ago-Iwoye to Ibadan and is one of the projects secured through the support of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu.

Abiodun further disclosed that his administration had awarded the reconstruction of the Ilishan–Ago-Iwoye–Ijebu-Igbo Road, as well as the Okun-Owa Road, Aiyepe–Odogbolu Road and Ikenne–Aiyepe Road.

“Help me to ask them if they have ever done even a kilometre of road?” the governor challenged, referring to opposition parties.

He said the APC’s record of performance had left the opposition with little to campaign with ahead of 2027.

“Anyone just making any baseless noise is just lying to you, because in 2019, they fell, in 2023, they also fell and I am certain that in 2027, they will also fail,” he said.

The governor also expressed optimism that Ogun would soon join the league of oil-producing states, while noting that the development of the Olokola Deep Sea Port and revival of the OKNLG project would further transform Ogun East and strengthen the state’s economy.

Abiodun commended President Tinubu for his support for Ogun State, particularly in the area of infrastructure, saying the President’s administration had demonstrated commitment to the development of the state.

He said he believed that the people of the South-West would support President Tinubu in 2027 based on his achievements in infrastructure and economic development.

“Every son and daughter of the South-West will vote for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu in 2027, not because he is a son of the soil, but because of his antecedents in developing the country in terms of infrastructural and economic development,” he said.

Earlier, the Ogun State APC Chairman, Chief Yemi Sanusi, attributed the influx of opposition members into the party to the performance of the Abiodun administration.

Sanusi assured the defectors that they would enjoy the same rights and privileges as existing members, while urging other opposition members to join the ruling party and contribute to the development of the state.

In his remarks, Asiwaju Oladapo Odumosu, a former PDP member, thanked Governor Abiodun for accepting him and his supporters into the APC, saying the administration’s performance and its accommodating disposition encouraged their decision to leave the opposition.

Other defectors, including Messrs Ladi Owoduni, Damilola Talabi, Sesan Odufuwa from Odogbolu, Wale Adeyemi from Ijebu-North, Seun Oguntimeyin from Ijebu-North-East, Sunday Taiwo from Remo North, Adewale Ismael from Ijebu-Igbo and former ADC Chairman in Ijebu-North-East, Hon. Erinle Opeoluwa, described Abiodun as an accommodating administrator who treats people equally irrespective of political affiliation.

Rotimi Okenla, who contested for the Ogun State House of Assembly under the PDP in 2019, said after 17 years in the opposition, he decided to join the APC because of the performance and accommodating nature of the Abiodun administration.

The defectors pledged their loyalty to the APC and vowed to work for the party’s victory in the 2027 general elections.

World.title: Why I left Kwara APC for PDP — Mustapha
World.content:
Saliu Mustapha

By Juliet Umeh

Senator Saliu Mustapha, representing Kwara Central Senatorial District in the National Assembly, has explained his decision to quit the All Progressives Congress, APC, for the Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, saying his defection was not a rejection of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu.

Mustapha, who recently emerged as the PDP candidate for Kwara Central through a substitution process, said he left the APC because of what he described as lack of consultation, internal democracy and sense of belonging under the leadership of Governor Abdulrahman Abdulrazaq.

Speaking on Channels Television, Mustapha said: “I have not dumped President Tinubu. Like the Honourable Minister of FCT said, this Rainbow Coalition has extended to Kwara too.

“That is why it was deliberate to pick the PDP as our platform. It is not just Senator Saliu Mustapha. It is as a result of the coalition of the Otoge Progressives, the G15 and the Elder Caucus.”

According to him, members of the groups became alienated by the manner in which the APC was being managed in the state.

He said: “We have all felt alienated from the way and manner Abdulrahman Abdulrazaq is running the APC in Kwara.”

Mustapha said his decision was also informed by the failure of the party leadership to adequately consult stakeholders ahead of the recent primaries.

“If there had been proper management and proper sense of belonging or consultation, we wouldn’t have gotten to this level,” he said.

The senator alleged that the APC primary process was flawed, describing it as a “sham”.

He said: “You announced that the primaries will start after the Jumu’ah prayers, and the results were announced by 4pm. How fast can they bring the results? When would the agents have arrived for them to do the coalition? It was a sham.”

Mustapha insisted that his movement to the PDP was not motivated by personal disappointment over the APC ticket.

“This is not a Saliu Mustapha decision. The entire group, the Otoge Progressives, had an agreement, a meeting and sharing formula with the PDP,” he said.

He also maintained that the coalition remained committed to President Tinubu’s 2027 ambition.

“I have not dumped President Tinubu,” Mustapha reiterated. “We are all supporting President Tinubu.”

On his expectations in the 2027 election, the senator expressed confidence that the coalition would defeat the APC in Kwara.

“I can assure you that in this election we are going for, we would have defeated Abdulrahman Abdurazaq by 12 o’clock,” he declared.

Mustapha said his ultimate objective was to “reset the political mood in Kwara” and restore wider consultation and inclusiveness in the state’s politics.

World.title: Arsenal beat Lampard’s Coventry 3-0 in Premier League opener
World.content:
Arsenal’s English winger, Bukayo Saka is substituted for Arsenal’s English midfielder, Noni Madueke during the English Premier League football match between Arsenal and Coventry City at the Emirates Stadium in London on August 21, 2026. Photo by Henry NICHOLLS / AFP.

Arsenal made the perfect start to their Premier League title defence with a stylish 3-0 win against Coventry in the opening game of the season on Friday.

Mikel Arteta’s side brushed aside promoted Coventry in emphatic fashion at the Emirates Stadium, underlining their determination to retain the title.

Kai Havertz struck early in the first half and Bukayo Saka doubled the lead before Martin Odegaard netted after the interval to complete Arsenal’s masterclass.

The Gunners have not successfully defended the English title since the 1930s, but Arteta insisted this week his players are hungry for more silverware.

Just 89 days after rounding off their title-winning campaign with a 2-1 victory at Crystal Palace in May, the champions showed no signs of being sated by that long-awaited triumph as they put Coventry to the sword.

The only downside for Arsenal was the realisation they have to wait 10 days for their next game at Aston Villa.

Worryingly for Arsenal’s rivals, they are only getting stronger and new signing Ezri Konsa was given a warm welcome when he was presented to fans before kick-off.

The England defender completed his £51 million ($69 million) move from Villa earlier on Friday and could make his debut against his old club on August 31.

Greek winger Christos Tzolis dazzled on his first league start for Arsenal after his close-season move from Club Brugge.

Fellow new signing Bruno Guimaraes was hardly missed after being sidelined by an injury suffered in last weekend’s Community Shield win over Manchester City.

Rampant Arsenal-

Coventry were playing their first Premier League game since 2001 after winning the Championship last season to end their long exile from the top-flight.

Having spent a season in the fourth tier, plunged into administration and twice been forced to ground-share away from Coventry in the 25 years since they were last in the Premier League, the return of Frank Lampard’s side was a feelgood moment.

But Arsenal had no room for sentiment as they dispatched Coventry in merciless style.

In their first home league game since being crowned champions last season, Arsenal strode onto the pitch with the acclaim of the sell-out 60,000 crowd ringing in their ears.

The party atmosphere created by Arsenal’s jubilant fans in north London was a fitting backdrop to a swaggering performance.

Tzolis, who provided two assists in the Community Shield, nearly bagged his first Arsenal goal in the opening minutes, firing just over from Odegaard’s pass.

He went close again moments later with a close-range effort that was cleared off the line by Bobby Thomas.

It was no surprise when Arsenal took the lead in ruthless fashion after 15 minutes.

Coventry defender Milan van Ewijk surrendered possession carelessly on the right flank and Riccardo Calafiori pounced, whipping in a cross that Havertz met with a clinical low strike from just inside the penalty area.

Arteta’s rampant team scented blood and went for the kill in the 23rd minute.

Rice and Odegaard exchanged passes to work the ball out to Tzolis, whose cross was pushed out by Coventry keeper Carl Rushworth into the path of Saka for a simple close-range finish.

Coventry had been reduced to helpless bystanders by Arsenal’s ceaseless pressing and clever movement.

If it was not already over, Odegaard put the result beyond doubt in the 49th minute.

Saka and Ben White teamed up to rip through the Coventry defence before Odegaard’s miscued shot from 10 yards scuffed past Rushworth’s weak attempted save.

Vanguard News

World.title: ICPC Uncovers Another Fake Agency, Tinubu Orders Arrest, Suspension of 3 Perm Secs
World.content:
*Nwabueze for arrest, Danjuma, Gagare, Pheelangwah suspended*Fake entity secured office inside SGF complex without presidential approval



*ICPC links discovery to probe of fictitious PFIPC



*President directs wider audit of MDAs, internal govt processes

Deji Elumoye in Abuja

President Bola Tinubu has ordered the immediate arrest of the promoter of another purported fake government agency and the suspension of three federal Permanent Secretaries following fresh findings by the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission (ICPC).

The ICPC Chairman, Dr Musa Adamu Aliyu, disclosed this to journalists in Abuja yesterday after briefing Tinubu on the commission’s latest findings.



Aliyu identified the three Permanent Secretaries ordered suspended by the President as M. S. Danjuma, Engr. Nadungu Gagare and Richard Pheelangwah.

He said the President also directed the immediate arrest of George Buchi Nwabueze, who allegedly promoted and operated the purported agency.
