World.title: Family worried for man missing since Melbourne shooting
World.content:
The loved ones of a Melbourne father who went missing after a shooting in the city's north-west say they hold grave fears for his welfare.

Police have been conducting a large-scale search for a 37-year-old man whom the ABC understands to be Khaled Malas.

Mr Malas, of Meadow Heights, has not been seen since August 19.

Investigators said he was allegedly shot in the chest that evening about 7:20pm after a dispute at a home in Wildwood.

Mohammed Aboueid, 56, has been charged with intentionally causing serious injury.

He appeared in the Melbourne Magistrates' Court on Friday night and is due to return in November.

The ABC understands the dispute allegedly has to do with a $500,000 debt.

Investigators said they held significant concerns for Mr Malas's welfare and that it was likely he had succumbed to his injuries.

A long-time friend of Mr Malas told the ABC he was a successful auto truck electrician.

He said family and friends feared the worst.

"It's such horrible news," the friend said.

"Khaled was a humble hard-working man that loved his young family, it's absolutely devastating."

Police are urging anyone with information to come forward.

World.title: Inside the libertarian city on a Caribbean island backed by Silicon Valley
World.content:
Alice Chen opens a glass door and leads the way past a wall of stickers bearing slogans such as "Make Death Optional" and "Live on Bitcoin". The room we've entered is part messy science lab, part share-house kitchen.

"Welcome to the Maker Space," Chen says. Sunlight peeks through palms swaying in the afternoon breeze outside, but what we've come to see lives in the windowless black tent sitting in the corner.

Chen unzips the door and retrieves a beaker from a small fridge inside.

"You can't find this anywhere else in the world," she says, holding up a vivid green liquid. This is what she came all the way from Canada to Próspera, a libertarian enclave on the Honduran island of Roatán, to develop — a live algae drink she says could add 20 years to your life.

"It's only possible here in Próspera because of their meta-regulatory framework," Chen says.

Alice Chen holding the live algae drink she's developing in Próspera. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Artworks on the walls in Próspera's shared working space. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

"Make death optional" is one of the slogans on display in the Maker Space. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

In Canada, where Chen was studying for her PhD, it would have taken months, if not years, to get approval to test the product.

"I would have been kicked out of any university even for just consuming it myself," she says.

So when she heard about the libertarian utopia in the Caribbean where she could bring it to life without those regulatory constraints, she dropped out and flew south.

In Próspera, businesses get to choose their own regulations from a menu of over 30 countries — or even propose new ones.

"We couldn't find any, so we created our own," says Alice, who's already assembled a small group of willing volunteers to test the product.

"The fact is, nowhere else in the world would regulators allow us to experiment, like, is this safe for human consumption, right?"

Chen's experiment is nothing out of the ordinary among the tight-knit group of biohackers, tech entrepreneurs and crypto bros who inhabit Próspera, a private city run by an American company. Próspera itself is a radical experiment, billed as "the future of human governance, privately run and for profit".

Roatán is a tourist island 60km off the coast of mainland Honduras. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

The Beta District was the first 58-acre parcel of land incorporated into the zone. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

So-called "startup cities" with light regulations, ultra-low taxes and minimal government oversight have long been a dream in online libertarian circles in the US. In Honduras, one of Latin America's poorest nations, it's become a reality. Próspera might be the most advanced test case for those libertarian ideas, which some hope to take global.

The project has the backing of America's tech elite. The Delaware-based company that runs the zone says it's raised almost $200 million in investment, including from venture capital firms linked to Silicon Valley billionaires Peter Thiel, Sam Altman and Marc Andreesen. Supporters say private cities like Próspera can help alleviate poverty in nations plagued by corruption and crime.

But in Honduras, where more than half the country lives in poverty, those claims have been the subject of fierce debate. The former government tried to shut Próspera down, claiming it was an affront to national sovereignty, offering little benefit to the nation. To its critics, it's an experiment gone dangerously wrong.

Duna Residences and the guard station along Próspera's main road. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Making its own laws

A boom gate halfway along the main road, manned by a smiling security guard with a handgun at his side, is the first real sign we're crossing into a parallel reality. Honduran law mostly ceases at the barrier gate. Beyond it, Próspera can make its own laws.

The guard checks that visitors have filled out the "agreement of co-existence", an online form binding them to the zone's system of private arbitration. Apart from criminal matters, cases are heard online by an Arizona-based panel of retired judges.

The Beta District, Próspera's main campus, is a sloping 58-acre plot fringed by palm trees and overlooking the Caribbean Sea. Calling it a "city" is generous, but there are plans to change that. For now, there's a a handful of buildings: a hostel, a robotic woodworking factory, and a futuristic-looking white dome giving off Fyre Festival vibes. There's a small shop where everything's bought with Bitcoin, the zone's preferred currency. Towering over all is Duna Residences, a gleaming 14-storey residential tower.

A robotic woodworking factory is staffed mostly by locals, Próspera says. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Duna Residences is home to about 45 permanent residents. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

A small hostel is among a handful of buildings in Próspera's main campus. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

A white dome is used to host events. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Closer to the beach, there's a restaurant and office complex, where we meet Erick Brimen, the Venezuelan-born former banker who founded Próspera in 2017.

"Really the whole thing started here, in this particular building," he says, sitting in a boardroom taking in views of the coral reef just offshore. "This was jungle before."

Próspera was created with the blessing of the Honduran government, after it legalised special jurisdictions known as ZEDEs — a Spanish acronym for Zones for Employment and Economic Development. Political instability and government corruption have long made Honduras toxic for foreign investment. The ZEDEs were meant to be the antidote.

A view from the restaurant over the coral reef. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Loading...

Brimen describes them as "pockets of stability" designed to lure foreign investors. Próspera's low tax rates are one of the big drawcards, with businesses paying as little as 1 per cent.

It's a formula he claims has already attracted 500 companies to the zone and created thousands of jobs.

"It's a poverty alleviation tool and an economic accelerant," Brimen says. "What we're doing here, I think, can lift people up from around the world by the billions."

Honduras first got the idea for the zones from a TED Talk. In a 2009 YouTube video, Paul Romer, who went on to become Chief Economist of the World Bank, argued "charter cities" run by stable foreign governments — think Canada or Norway — could help lift developing nations out of poverty.

But the model Honduras went on to adopt bore little resemblance to Romer's vision, allowing foreign companies to run the zones with an extraordinary degree of autonomy.

Próspera has the power to create its own legal system, courts, police force, tax code and regulations — even set its own building code. Duna tower would have been illegal to build anywhere else on the island.

"The zoning outside caps you at 12 stories," says Brimen, as we scale the steps at the base of the tower. "And indeed, those extra stories were authorised through the internal approval process."

The fight to shut it down

Some critics have denounced Próspera as a "state within a state". Fernando Garcia, a former minister for the economy in the left-wing Libre party, says it undermines Honduras's national sovereignty.

"It's totally affected," he says. "A state has three components: government, population and territory. All three are affected by Próspera. The libertarians want the states of the world in their current form to disappear."

He also disputes the idea Próspera is generating wealth for Hondurans. Even by Próspera's own reckoning, only about 30 companies are physically present in the zone, a fact Garcia seizes on.

"What [the companies] do is turn Próspera into a tax haven for tax evasion in their countries of origin," he says. "They don't live there or generate any activity there. They generate it in their countries of origin."

Fernando Garcia was given a special presidential commission under the previous government to shut down Honduras's ZEDEs. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Garcia believes Próspera undermines Hondras's national sovereignty. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Erick Brimen dismisses the suggestion the city is doing anything wrong.

"In Próspera, there are taxes and people must pay them, and there are regulations and people must follow them," he says.

Próspera pays 12 per cent of the taxes and fees it collects to the Honduran government, and Brimen says there's evidence it's already bringing in new investment.

The libertarian experiment on a Caribbean island backed by Silicon Valley Watch Foreign Correspondent's Paraside Inc. on ABC iview.

In 2022, Fernando Garcia was brought in by the leftist government of Xiomara Castro to shut Próspera down. The government set about repealing the laws that made the ZEDEs legal.

In response, Próspera launched legal action against the state of Honduras for $US10.7 billion — roughly a third of GDP — in a move Garcia says was akin to "blackmail". Ultimately, his effort to rid the country of its ZEDEs was a lost cause.

Libre was turfed out of office in national elections last December, which saw the right-wing Nationals returned to power — the party that ushered Próspera into existence in the first place.

That election, decided on a margin of just 1 per cent, remains a source of much contention in Honduras. Garcia claims it was "stolen" by a man with a renewed interest in the Western hemisphere, and a desire to "consolidate the position of libertarians in Honduras" — Donald Trump.

The US president made an extraordinary intervention in the fiercely contested poll, publicly backing the National Party and pardoning its jailed former leader, Juan Orlando Hernandez, days before Hondurans cast their ballots. Those actions are widely seen as having tipped the scales for his preferred party to win.

An outer suburb of Tegucigalpa, the capital of Honduras. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Gang crime and lack of opportunity have driven many from the Honduran capital. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Some say safeguarding the future of Próspera might have had something to do with it. Trump had been publicly and privately lobbied by his long-time advisor Roger Stone, who penned a blog post urging the president to pardon Hernandez in order to "crush socialism" and "save" the "freedom city".

One of the world's foremost experts on Central America, Chris Sabatini, believes Stone was doing the bidding of a group of libertarian tech bros.

"They're an emerging, very powerful bloc of political activists that are basically funded to the teeth and are willing to step out and start to push their own agenda," he says.

Brimen is coy about the president's intervention, merely saying that Trump was trying to make the region more "stable and prosperous" and that the development deserved the support it received.

Regardless of the president's knowledge of or support for Próspera, Sabitini says his actions have "basically guaranteed that Próspera will remain … as long as Donald Trump is in the White House".

The view from the pool deck on Duna Tower. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

A city of the future

Expansion is now the goal. From the pool deck on Duna tower, Brimen points over a nearby hill towards Pristine Bay, a sprawling resort and golf course that's been incorporated into the zone.

ZEDEs can add territories and they don't even need to be connected, and according to Brimen Próspera is a patchwork of some 1,000 acres, including a port on the Honduran mainland at La Ceiba, with a total area larger than Monaco.

In time, he believes the population could reach 100,000.

"If you think, in 20, 30 years' time, it's very feasible," Brimen says.

For now though, it's eerily quiet. Próspera claims 1,700 people have filled out an online residency form, but only about 200 people actually live here permanently. One of them is Rich Lee, who's among the 45 or so permanent residents in Duna tower.

He moved here from the US about two years ago, after a death in the family caused him to reconsider things.

"There were a lot of people here and it was really happening," Lee says. "There was a lot of really awesome projects, bleeding-edge stuff.

"I thought, 'This is what I need' — you know, 'I'm kind of starved for this right now.' So I moved out here."

The golf course and resort at Pristine Bay has been incorporated into the zone. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

An old restaurant is now a Bitcoin education centre. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Even the swimwear is Bitcoin-themed in Próspera. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Lee came to turn his biohacking hobby into a startup business. Standing in the Maker Space, he shows off his implants, of which there are seven in total, including a chunky tap-to-pay credit card chip under the skin in the back of his right hand.

He has Bluetooth headphones permanently implanted and magnets in his fingertips to "touch an otherwise invisible world of electro-magnetic fields."

It's also a handy pub trick. "Honestly, this has got me so much free beer," Lee says, dangling a bottle cap from the tip of his finger.

In the US, body modification tech is a legal grey area, Lee says, and unlikely to attract the hefty financial backing needed to pass FDA approvals. He believes the US system of regulation is broken.

"The idea that regulation in the US is making things safer, I think, is kind of a fallacy. Currently it takes about a billion dollars to bring a pharmaceutical or, like, a gene therapy, to market, and about 10 years," Lee says.

"So we're at this weird place where we've painted ourselves into the corner with regulations in a lot of cases."

Loading...

A "taser knife", an invention used for sport in Próspera. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

A biohacking-themed artwork in the Maker Space. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Lee isn't the only biohacker to find his way to Próspera. This is where the ultra-wealthy longevity guru Bryan Johnson came to receive an unregulated gene therapy for the 2025 Netflix documentary Don't Die.

Medical experimentation has become one of the zone's hallmarks. But billionaire celebrities are a rarity, according to Lee.

"I think there's this fantasy that it's this inaccessible place for elites that are, you know, doing crazy experiments on this anarchist island. But we're just people out here and we're definitely not billionaires," he says.

Later that evening, a handful of residents gather in the Maker Space for a weekly games night. Many believe Próspera's doing good for the island.

"Most people don't come here to do anything except laze around and build a nice house and buy a boat," says Jason, another resident biohacker.

"But when you start to talk to people about, we're pushing forward science, we're going to put in regenerative medicine, ears start perking up."

An island of opposition

Not all the locals agree. Just along the beach from Próspera is the old fishing village of Crawfish Rock, which gets its name from the spiny lobster that once flourished here. It's an English-speaking community of about 600, tracing its roots back to British colonial days. People here are split over the private city next door.

Vanessa Cardenas, a community leader whose family has lived here for five generations, is one of its most vocal critics.

"No-one ever expected this kind of situation to ever occur," she says.

"For them to come and say they want to build a country in my country, where they have their own laws, regulations, their everything — they don't pay the taxes I pay and I'm from here. It's preposterous. I mean, it makes no sense."

The village of Crawfish Rock is Próspera's nearest neighbour. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Vanessa Cardenas is one of the most vocal critics. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Residents of Crawfish Rock in church. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Cardenas acknowledges that Próspera has provided jobs for the community, but says that has deepened divisions.

"There's a lack of trust now," she says."Because if you're working with them, you're getting a salary, so they're good to you. But then there's us, we're seeing the danger. I can't trust you or talk with you about certain things, so it has caused some division."

Cardenas worries about a return to the village's colonial past.

"Our country has ever been explored and our riches taken for somewhere else. It has never stayed for the Honduran people," she says.

That's a charge Erick Brimen rejects.

"It's the opposite," he says.

"It's a government choosing to liberate its people from the shackles of poor regulatory and legal environments by partnering voluntarily with partners that are capable to provide better conditions. So colonialism is exactly the opposite of what we're doing."

Exporting the movement

Back in Próspera, there's a broad gash in the green hillside behind Duna tower where the next big residential development is taking shape. The tangled jungle has been hacked back to make way for five squat, European-style apartment buildings.

"I've been looking into building a similar thing in Portugal," says Ivan Syrtsov, the young Ukrainian who's developing the site.

"Permit-wise, it would take me approximately four years. Over here, it's two weeks."

Young Ukrainian property developer Ivan Syrtzov is building a residential complex, pictured on the screen behind him. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

Construction of five new apartment buildings is moving forward at a rapid pace. (Foreign Correspondent: Matt Henry)

He didn't even need to consult the council before breaking ground — just a private insurance company.

"It's interested in making money, right? And if that's the case, then they try to make a rapid review of the project and work as efficiently as possible," Syrtsov says.

But he is here with more than just a quick-hit real estate project in mind. He got interested in Próspera at a "Network State" conference, where speakers discussed building new cities around alternative models of governance. If it succeeds here in Honduras, he plans to take the idea global.

"I would really love to build a city of my own," Syrtsov says. "So, become competition of Próspera."

It's a vision shared by Brimen, who believes "countries all around the world are going to want to emulate" his model city.

"Anything that works to lift people up can and should be replicated," he says.

For Fernando Garcia, it's all the more reason to keep fighting to put an end to Próspera.

"In Honduras, the battle against the libertarians of the world is being waged," he says.

"This is the spearhead."

Watch Foreign Correspondent's journey through Próspera on YouTube or ABC iview now.

World.title: US mum was 'begging for help' before killing children, family testifies
World.content:
In October 2022, Lindsay Clancy messaged her mother:

"Mom, will you please come up and stay with me for a bit? I'm really sick. Something is wrong."

Warning: This story contains details that may be distressing for some readers.

Ms Clancy was a former labour and delivery nurse known as a dedicated and loving mother to three children aged five and under.

But her mental health had begun to decline after the birth of her third son, Callan.

Despite repeatedly seeking help from medical professionals, she continued to report a poor mental state.

By December, she had confessed to her mother and then-husband that she had thoughts of harming her children.

A few weeks later, Ms Clancy had killed all three children and attempted to end her own life.

Clancy was 'begging for help', family says

On January 24, 2023, Ms Clancy took her daughter, Cora, to a doctor's appointment and sent her then-husband, Patrick Clancy, photos of their children throughout the day.

When Mr Clancy returned home later that day after running errands, he discovered Ms Clancy lying paralysed in their backyard.

Lindsay Clancy jumped from the bedroom window of the family home after killing her children. (Reuters: CJ Gunther/Pool)

He found their two eldest children dead from strangulation in the family basement. Callan, who was eight months old at the time, died in hospital a few days later.

Whether Ms Clancy killed her children is not in dispute at her triple-murder trial currently underway in the US state of Massachusetts.

US mum on trial for murder says voice told her to 'kill the children' A mother who says she was suffering postpartum psychosis when she killed her three children and attempted to take her own life is now on trial for their murder.

Her defence lawyer, Kevin Reddington, argues she was a loving mother who was overcome by postpartum psychosis, a rare mental illness linked to the stress, sleep deprivation and hormonal changes that follow childbirth.

He says Ms Clancy repeatedly sought help from medical professionals and was prescribed several psychiatric medications that made her spiral "out of control".

When her family testified for the defence this week, they described a woman who was anxious, paranoid and suicidal.

Ms Clancy's mother, Paula Musgrove, said on Monday she often stayed with her daughter between October and December 2022.

She said Ms Clancy was afraid of sleeping alone and believed the medications she was taking "were destroying her mind".

The jury was shown a text message Lindsay Clancy sent her mother about her declining mental health. (AP: Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/Pool)

Her former mother-in-law, Susan Clancy, testified on Tuesday that Ms Clancy had been "begging for help" in the months leading up the killings.

"Lindsay was struggling; we were all concerned," she said.

The jury was shown texts between the two in which Ms Clancy spoke about fears she had developed a dependence on benzodiazepines and could not sleep without taking them.

"I'm not okay and I'm terrified of taking meds tonight," Lindsay texted her mother-in-law on November 30, 2022.

Disputed picture of mental health

Earlier in the trial, the jury heard Ms Clancy had sought treatment for severe mental health problems, including admitting herself to a psychiatric hospital.

But witnesses also noted Ms Clancy would not always take the medications prescribed to help with her insomnia, anxiety and depression, and that she expressed fears she was addicted to some of them.

'His little face turned into a dragon': One mother's experience of postnatal psychosis Ariane Beeston worked as a child protection officer, the vicarious trauma of that work impacted her when she had a child of her own.

The defence has argued that Ms Clancy was over-medicated and that her care was disjointed, with doctors not speaking to one another or sharing notes.

The defence also showed she was discharged from one facility after just one day and denied a higher level of care at another when she could not show she had a suicide plan.

Prosecutors questioned the seriousness of Ms Clancy's suicide attempt and showed through texts and photos that she performed many normal activities the day of the killings, including taking her children to the doctor and playing with them in the snow.

Her doctors have testified they never saw Ms Clancy exhibit signs of mania or psychosis, though she did repeatedly talk of feeling suicidal.

Psychologist Paul Zeizel testified that he found no evidence Lindsay Clancy was faking psychiatric symptoms. (AP: Amanda Sabga/The Boston Herald/Pool)

Paul Zeizel, a clinical and forensic psychologist who spent more than 35 hours with Ms Clancy over dozens of visits and reviewed her medical records, said he found no evidence she was faking or exaggerating psychiatric symptoms.

He testified that psychotic symptoms could come and go, and that a person experiencing psychosis can still perform ordinary activities such as making a phone call or driving a car.

On cross-examination, prosecutors pointed out mistakes Dr Zeizel made in his report about Ms Clancy and questioned whether he could be objective about her diagnosis when he was seeing her as a patient and working with the defence, including by appearing at a news conference with Mr Reddington.

Clancy faces life without parole

Ms Clancy has not testified and is not required to do so, but jurors have seen her break down in sobs at several points, including when prosecutors showed the jury autopsy photos of the children.

If convicted of murder, Ms Clancy faces life in prison without parole.

If found not guilty because of a lack of criminal responsibility, she would be committed to a state mental health facility.

ABC/AP

World.title: AFL LIVE: Lethal says Pies should take decision out of Pendles’ hands; Blues in charge at Marvel
World.content:
AFL great Leigh Matthews says it would be wrong for Collingwood to allow Scott Pendlebury to make his own call on his playing future, declaring the Magpies needed to deliver honest feedback.

Pendlebury, 38, was hurt in the Magpies’ 63-point loss to Brisbane on Friday night, finishing the contest on the bench with a knee bursa issue, that is swelling near the joint.

Scott Pendlebury walks from the ground with his Collingwood playing future in doubt. Getty Images

The Magpies also have concerns the former skipper has a hamstring strain, scans to confirm whether he has any chance to play in next weekend’s wildcard round.

Should Pendlebury not play and the Magpies lose, the league’s all-time games record holder may have suited up for the last time at Collingwood, for he does not have a contract for next season.

He is set to become an unrestricted free agent, with several clubs linked to his services if he opts to play elsewhere in 2027.

Magpies president Barry Carp said on Friday night that the choice was in Pendlebury’s hands, but Matthews, the 1990 Magpies premiership coach, said any decision should largely be the club’s call.

“Not in my opinion, it’s never the player’s call,” Matthews told 3AW on Saturday.

“But Scott Pendlebury is a high-class person. If [coach] Craig McRae and the football people said: ‘We think it’s probably time’, I think he would accept that. And that’s the way the conversation should go.

“But a player just can’t say: ‘I want to play, I don’t care if you don’t think I am up to it, I just want to play and I want a contract.’

“But even Barry Carp, I don’t think he would go that far. I think if the football department said: ‘No, we just think it’s time’, I probably suspect Scott Pendlebury would accept that himself.

“It’s a joint conversation but it can’t be unilaterally the player decides, otherwise he would play until he is 50.“

Pendlebury has said if his body feels fine, he would commit to playing on. The Gold Coast Suns and Essendon have been linked to the two-time premiership player, the latter in a deal which could have him become an assistant coach.

Matthews said the Magpies’ coaches would need to be honest with Pendlebury.

“It should be a choice but sometimes players have to be told what you are observing from those who are running the team,” Matthews said. “You try to do it diplomatically but you also have to be honest and say, and use Scott as an example: ‘We think it’s time, we don’t want to be playing half a year in the reserves’, for instance. I think most players would accept that from their coaches.

The Magpies will play either Carlton or the Western Bulldogs next weekend. Pendlebury’s finals campaign last year ended early in the preliminary final when he strained a calf.

World.title: ‘Scorched earth for satire’: How this former ambassador’s show was scuppered by Trump
World.content:
Exclusive NationalComedy ‘Scorched earth for satire’: How this former ambassador’s show was scuppered by Trump Stephen Brook August 22, 2026 — 1:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Diplomats never tell, but a new dark TV comedy created by the former Australian ambassador to France promises to be anything but discreet. Brendan Berne, our man in Paris from 2017 to 2020, has just filmed the pilot for a sitcom called Rank, inspired by his two decades of service with the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade. Brendan Berne (left), pictured with French President Emmanuel Macron, is a former ambassador now focused on creative projects. Berne, 56, who resigned from DFAT in 2020 to move to Burgundy in France with his husband and to concentrate on creative projects, describes Rank as “The Thick of It updated for the age of Trump, Truss and Thunberg”. Networks and production houses were interested, but then the US president sued the BBC for defamation and, long story short, corporations shied away from a pointed comedy in the era of Donald Trump, Liz Truss’ short stint as UK prime minister and eco-warrior Greta Thunberg.



“Trump suing the BBC has scorched the earth for political satire, and the joke invigilators and sensitivity readers make transgressive comedy challenging. Five years on, someone laughed it’s been my Odyssey, but I’d say it’s more been the Plodyssey,” Berne says. “When the rights returned to me, I revisited my more provocative scripts, which resonated with investors, and we have just finished shooting the pilot.” As Australia’s ambassador, Berne helped to persuade French President Emmanuel Macron to visit Australia – a first. And in 2017, when Australia’s marriage equality legislation became law, he started a video on social media discussing stronger relations between Australia and France and ended it with him proposing to his Swiss-Australian partner of 11 years, Thomas Marti. Millions in France viewed it on social media, which led to Berne appearing on France’s top TV talk show. Rank is not Berne’s only project. He has helped to develop a cello concerto that tells the largely lost story of a 19th-century French cabin boy being adopted by an Aboriginal tribe on the Cape York Peninsula.



Melissa King, the director of artistic planning for the Sydney Symphony Orchestra (SSO), commissioned the work, by composer Matthew Hindson. It was developed with the support of the Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies and is scheduled to premiere in NAIDOC Week next year. The concerto will bring to life the largely untold story of 14-year-old Narcisse Pelletier, who was abandoned by his ship’s crew in Far North Queensland in 1858 and adopted by the Uutaalnganu people, with whom he lived for 17 years. The cast of Rank (from left): Phillip Honeywell, Bryan Williams, Felicity Bown, Jodyanne Fletcher Richardson, Dana Blacklake and Will Frazer. “This an important concerto for the SSO, as it brings the story of Narcisse and the Uutaalnganu to a wider audience, the first major cultural project dedicated to this incredible true story,” King says. Berne and French cellist Sebastien Hurtaud, who hails from the same place as Pelletier, travelled last September to the Cape York Peninsula and met members of the Uutaalnganu people, some of whom still had oral accounts of Pelletier passed down from the 19th century. While visiting, Hurtaud played part of the composition for locals.



“They still share stories of the para (white man) who they saved in 1858 and who became part of them. One young woman recounted to me the story of Narcisse killing a crocodile after it had taken a baby, earning the respect of his new community,” Berne says. Pelletier was later returned to France against his wishes, and his parents forced him to undertake an exorcism. Berne (right) and husband Thomas Marti in Paris. “As a former ambassador to France, I believed this forgotten chapter of the France-Australia relationship needed to be told, especially as the Indigenous people were the hero of the story,” Berne says. “I also hoped it might help salve some of the wounds in the immediate wake of the cancellation of the submarine program in a country where culture means a tremendous amount.”



The French embassy in Australia appointed Berne to the French-Australian Culture Exchange Foundation, which is chaired in Melbourne by Myriam Boisbouvier-Wylie. Related Article Foreign relations Trump, subs and the Iran war: Australia’s replacement for Rudd has arrived in DC Berne’s TV program had a circuitous route to existence. In 2022, it was ranked in the top three of a co-production pitching competition, Series Mania, an international TV industry festival staged annually in Lille. In developing the project, he worked with executive producer Glen Condie, the Emmy Award-nominated producer of Top End Wedding. Rank, billed as a comedy of diplomatic proportions, was written by Berne and should appeal to disillusioned Gen Xers. It is set in a fictional South Pacific country, where British diplomats decide to give asylum to a rogue state weapons scientist in a misguided attempt to celebrate women in science week. The team is then thrown into turmoil by the appearance of a bumbling British minister.



The program will be released in December and is available on rankthecomedy.com. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

France Stephen Brook is a special correspondent for The Age and CBD columnist for The Age and The Sydney Morning Herald. He was previously deputy editor of The Sunday Age. He is a former media editor of The Australian and spent six years in London working for The Guardian. or email. Connect via X

World.title: ‘On the next adventure’: Renovators sell inner-city Edwardian for $1,385,000
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions ‘On the next adventure’: Renovators sell inner-city Edwardian for $1,385,000 Wes Mountain August 22, 2026 — 1:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A two-bedroom Edwardian in Richmond, directly across from Bicentennial Park, sold for $1,385,000 at auction on Saturday – $65,000 above its reserve. The home at 20 Parkville Street sits in a row of red-brick terraces looking onto the park. It maintains original exterior features such as tessellated tile paths and stained-glass windows, and has an updated interior featuring high ceilings, open-plan living and new appliances. It had a price guide of $1.2 million to $1.32 million, and a reserve of $1.32 million. Jellis Craig Richmond agent and auctioneer Luke Schickerling said strong bidding opened at $1.2 million, the bottom of the guide, and went up quickly in $10,000 increments before hitting $1.32 million and being declared on the market.



Related Article Exclusive

Melbourne house prices How much it costs to live in Melbourne’s most desired school zones From there, three potential buyers continued to trade bids until the home sold to a young couple, who Schickerling said were new to the Richmond area. The vendors were renovators, who he said were now “onto the next adventure”. He said the property had performed well, and there were more people bidding than he would have expected just a few weeks ago, as the market was starting to warm up for spring – traditionally the peak period for auctions in Melbourne – and fewer properties were coming up for sale than expected. “We have the lowest stock levels I can recall in recent memory,” Schickerling said. The preserved Edwardian features at the front of the property conceal a modern, spacious interior. Jellis Craig Richmond



The property was one of 598 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne this week. In Brunswick, a warehouse conversion apartment – in the same building known to be the home of Nina Proudman in the TV series Offspring – sold for $1,126,000 at auction, soaring $126,000 above its $1 million reserve. The light-filled two-bedroom apartment at 210/1-3 Dods Street, complete with quirky egg-yolk yellow central bathroom, expansive open-plan living, dining and storage areas, and a north-facing view to Brunswick’s churches and rooftops, had a price guide of $950,000 to $1 million. Nelson Alexander Brunswick agent Janine Ballantyne said auctioneer James Pilliner opened bidding at $970,000, before four bidders pushed it easily past the $1 million mark in $10,000 increments.



From there, the bidders winnowed down to three to take the price up to $1.1 million, and then down to two as the increments grew smaller and the auction came to a close. The buyer was a professional moving into the area. The egg-yolk yellow central bathroom, askew in its own box within the apartment’s expansive interior, was just one characterful element of the warehouse conversion. Nelson Alexander Brunswick The vendor had decided to upsize within Brunswick after 21 years in the stylish apartment. Ballantyne said the result was indicative of the market. “[It’s] price-sensitive, but if people can see value, they will engage,” she said. “It doesn’t feel as though we are going to have the usual levels of spring stock, whether that puts pressure on prices or not remains to be seen.”

World.title: ‘It’s like we’re being robbed’: The relentless march of data centres
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Dublin: The sun is setting over the rolling fields near a small town in Ireland as Sorcha O’Neill and Dolores Moore point towards a large stretch of farmland that is meant to be bulldozed to make way for a row of data centres. We are standing at the edge of their suburb in Naas, a centuries-old town in County Kildare, at an old fence covered in blackberry bushes. Within weeks, they fear, their council will approve the next step in building the data factories of the internet age. “We were never informed about this,” says O’Neill, a former local councillor who understands the planning system. Only four weeks earlier, she tells me, she was checking plans for a more distant data centre when she noticed the paperwork for the farmland in an area known as Jigginstown. Sorcha O’Neill stands near a Microsoft data centre at Castle Grange Business Park in Ireland. She and her neighbours are worried about a similar project being built near their homes in Naas, in County Kildare. David Crowe Her heart sank. “That’s right next door.” Now the two neighbours have joined the agonising debate in Ireland about the scale of these new projects. The country already has about 72 data centres and is forecast to have dozens more in only a few years because it is so attractive for developers. It has skilled workers, low company tax rates, a cool climate and good land. Most importantly, it has the location. The facilities here, close to the high-speed lines that connect Europe to America, can quickly crunch data for artificial intelligence applications being used by businesses and consumers in the world’s wealthiest nations. Already, these facilities use one-fifth of the electricity from the nation’s grid. Soon it will be one-third. That makes Ireland a test case in the march of the data centres.



O’Neill and Moore discovered too late that Kildare County Council had zoned the land next to their homes for data centre use by the owner, Microsoft. That decision, made without fanfare several years ago, now makes it very difficult for them to challenge the outcome and ensure the land is zoned only for agriculture, as it was for years. Moore, a former catering worker, has been in this community since 1995. “I moved here from Dublin to make a better life for my children,” she says. “And my kids loved it here.” Now she worries about the construction noise from the project and the changes when the data centres are built. O’Neill, a tech worker, talks about the scale of the project when we drive around the perimeter of the farmland, passing horse studs and an old canal. “Who’s going to want to buy to live next to a data centre?” she asks. The rolling fields in Waterford could soon be hosting enormous data centres. Nobody in this community knows how big the data centres may be because those plans are yet to be unveiled. For many, the goal is to stop the plans at a council meeting on September 9, before the developers take the next step. A short drive away, just off the motorway into Dublin, stands a sign of things to come. The Grange Castle Business Park hosts tech giants including Amazon, Google and Microsoft. It is also home to a vast Pfizer facility that makes medicines for global markets – a high-tech contrast to the old pubs and traditional music found in Dublin’s city centre. O’Neill stops outside a long row of white buildings at Site 075. There are no logos on the fence, but this is Microsoft’s address. And it is a future O’Neill does not want in her backyard.



Demand for data is soaring as people use more AI. The Grange Castle data centre complex is Microsoft’s largest outside the United States, consuming 1.3 million megawatt hours of electricity last year, according to its latest environmental report. To put that in perspective, the Microsoft data centre in Sydney consumed only 7704 megawatt hours. Related Article Data centres ‘Difficult to reconcile’: The Australian council moving to ban data centres Microsoft is building a new gas-fired power station to support the Irish site and take some of the load off the national electricity grid. It is also vowing to minimise water use. Each year, the Castle Grange facility uses the equivalent of seven Olympic swimming pools – very low compared to the 392 used by the company’s data centre in Phoenix, Arizona. (The Sydney facility used three last year.) As demand grows, Microsoft needs more space. That is why it is working on the Jigginstown project. The precinct is 54.55 hectares – bigger than the Royal Botanic Gardens in Melbourne (38 hectares) and in Sydney (30 hectares). The company says 37 hectares will be set aside for new parklands, including a boardwalk and a walking track. This is not enough to mollify local residents – especially when O’Neill sees the size of the buildings at Grange Castle. The challenge for Ireland, however, is that it wants more growth in the tech industries that set up there during the nation’s “Celtic Tiger” economic revival in the 1990s, helping to lift living standards. Swimming against the tide



Critics say the data centres use too much power and water without creating enough jobs or paying enough economic dividends to local communities. But they are wrong on all counts, according to Ronan Kelly, the chief executive of Digital Infrastructure Ireland, an industry group that represents companies that build and operate these facilities. “The world is in a wave of investment in the data centre space at the moment, which is underpinned by the wave of investment in the AI sector in general, and that won’t last forever,” he says. “When this wave of investment in the AI space stops, the data centres that have capacity will capture the workloads for the next 20, 30 or 40 years. With that will come the taxation from the revenues that flow through them. With that will come the high-skilled jobs to continue to develop and adapt those facilities for emerging workloads.” Loading Ireland has a natural advantage with data centre location, positioned as it is between the US and Europe. Latency, measured in the milliseconds it takes to get a response from an AI app or an online service, is its strength. A facility in Ireland can deliver faster speeds for multiple applications talking to each other across continents, and Kelly believes this will be vital for “agentic AI”, where the apps are increasingly autonomous. Australia, located at the end of the world’s data lines, is unlikely to be able to offer this kind of low latency. For Kelly and the data centre companies he represents, there is a limited time for Ireland to ride this economic wave. He rejects the argument that the projects are vast spaces without workers, pointing to the jobs that are created to build and operate them. This includes the creation of specialist Irish companies that develop power and cooling systems for projects in and outside the country.



The Irish government has data to back these claims, courtesy of a report it commissioned from KPMG, received in June, which estimated that Irish-owned high-tech construction generated €2.1 billion ($3.4 billion) in exports in the data centre business in 2024. Related Article Explainer

Data centres Underwater, in space and in your city: Behind the data centre boom From 2010 to 2014, it found, the sector created about 17,000 jobs directly. This comprised 9356 additional construction jobs and 7636 operational jobs. Even if the building boom eased over time, KPMG said, the tax benefits would continue to flow from this workforce. Over five years to 2030, it estimated this would be worth €1.36 billion to the government. When KPMG looked at the broadest possible benefits of digital infrastructure, it claimed this part of the economy supported 876,000 jobs and €14.6 billion in annual employment-related tax in 2024 alone. Stopping this growth, says Kelly when we meet in Dublin, means letting other countries gain the jobs instead. “If you look at the backdrop of the world today, where they talk about AI, it is going to have a significant impact on the number of jobs that are out there,” he says. “Sending capacity overseas is really dangerous. You need to look 10, 20 or 50 years out to consider all the implications of this. Any short-term decisions taken today can have really damaging long-term implications.” Feeding the AI beast

World.title: The Swans are nothing without the W: Why I’ll be at the SCG on Sunday
World.content:
NationalAFL off-field behaviour Opinion The Swans are nothing without the W: Why I’ll be at the SCG on Sunday

Victoria Rawlings August 22, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s been a hard week to be a Swans supporter, especially as a woman. The horror of headlines on Monday and Tuesday about some of our most revered players has led to a reckoning of who we are and what we can support. While police investigations are ongoing, the details that are emerging are both damning and distressing. Victoria Rawlings is a former AFLW field umpire and passionate Swans supporter. Stefanie Zingsheim As a researcher in gendered violence, and a passionate Swans supporter, this has been a particularly challenging experience. Like many supporters, I have long seen the Swans as leaders in social justice and progressive issues in the AFL. They are the Pride Round club, and this year took a stand against another club’s inaction and hypocrisy around homophobia. They create a home ground experience that is incredibly inclusive and oriented to welcome all. From this baseline, the best word to define my feelings this week has been betrayal. In many ways, I was foolish enough to think the Swans were different. But really, I should have paid more attention to my own two-decade experience as an AFL player, administrator, umpire and fan. The signs of exclusion and hostility were there as a girl; there was no pathway for me to play football, so it never even appeared on my radar. We were framed as incapable, too delicate, not interested, or not active enough to have leagues warranted for us. Many current and past AFLW players continue to share this narrative.



The signs were there when I finally played in the Sydney Women’s Australian Football League, as it was then known, a group of teams from around Sydney that played a league that was run by women, for women. Even then, it was hard to find space and time for training that didn’t clash with the favoured men’s teams. At Sydney University, we trained on a grass hockey square, despite our games being played at large oval grounds. This, I was told, was a huge improvement from just a couple of years prior, where volunteers had to bring temporary Auskick posts to set up games on “cow paddock” fields each weekend. Victoria Rawlings umpiring a game of AFL. Stefanie Zingsheim They were there when I worked in a club administrator job in Sydney. They were keen to have a “ladies’ day”, not for the players of the adjacent women’s club, but for the wives and girlfriends of the men’s players. As I pitched the idea of fundraising for a charity that focused on violence against women, I was told that it was a bit grim, and we should go for the more palatable concern of breast cancer. The message? Men’s violence against women exists elsewhere, and is not our concern. They were there as I umpired for around 10 years, where both personally and structurally, I was subjected to elements that make girls and women understand that they are, and always will be, outsiders. My research on the experience of female umpires in Australian football showed that this was not an individual experience, but a systemic issue, and one that the AFL has been slow to address. While I’m not suggesting that these experiences are commensurate or comparable to the harms of sexual assault, they speak to a broader positioning of women as lesser, as peripheral, and of not warranting equal respect in football spaces. Coupled with “jokes” or “banter” that are difficult to act against, these are the seeds that grow into incidents of sexual violence. We might see the eventual outcomes as unintelligible, but they have been fostered through countless interactions that diminish the value and humanity of women.



Of course there have been incredible moments of hope and triumph – the establishment and expansion of the AFLW, the well-attended games at Henson Park, the increasing visibility and pay of these athletes and those who participate in the league. However, the challenges are ongoing. This battle has had dramatic costs this week, with women again understanding the ways that sexism, objectification, and misogyny operate away from public eyes. Our thoughts are with those women as they navigate what is likely to be a horrific experience at protecting their privacy and their mental and emotional health. Related Article Opinion

AFL off-field behaviour Men run the AFL and it is time they fixed its dark underbelly Angela Pippos Contributor As Angela Pippos and Kate McCarthy argued earlier in the week, this horror is compounded by the incredibly jarring use of passive language around sexual assault, like “players found themselves in this situation” from Matthew Pavlich, the CEO of the Swans. It is unacceptable that any statement on sexual violence does not centre the women who have been harmed. And it is unacceptable that we are not attentive to the women players and staff in this club who will have had the rug pulled out from under them again as they see and hear about disrespectful, objectifying and dehumanising behaviours from their colleagues. Like so many this week I have been doing some soul-searching about whether to attend Sunday’s match. I was always, of course, going to attend the AFLW game. This is our time to show that the Swans are nothing without W. But I am also, with great apprehension, seeking to open myself up to supporting the remainder of the men’s Swans squad as they take the field later in the afternoon.



The five players allegedly involved in this case have been stood down, and that is the only correct step that the club could take to signal their institutional obligations and commitments to rightfully furious and disappointed fans. Coach Dean Cox and Captain Callum Mills fronted the media on Friday, and the latter started with an apology “to the AFLW players, our female staff, and the women in our lives, our partners, mothers, sisters, and all women in the community”. His words, though likely carefully crafted, seemed genuinely heartfelt, as he expressed that he was “deeply shocked and disappointed to be here”, and that as a playing group they fully supported the club’s suspension of the players involved. These words matter. And it’s the club’s approach to saying them that have convinced me that it’s possible to both carry disappointment, rage, and betrayal, but also to show up with some care and openness for the other players on the team. Perhaps we can show them that we, too, are part of their team. Women and girls have managed to sustain our relationship with football through many hostilities, and it’s through our commitment to this love of the game that we are seeing the painstakingly slow work of cultural change. By our voices being loud in membership, play, administration, and officiating, perhaps we can hang on to this game that we love, and perhaps one day, it will love us back. Victoria Rawlings is an associate professor in the Sydney School of Education and Social Work. She conducts research about gender, sexuality, and schooling, and is a former AFLW and NEAFL field umpire. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Alleged sexual assault victim from Swans late-night party plans civil action
World.content:
A woman who alleges she was the victim of a sexual assault during a late-night party with five Sydney Swans players in a Melbourne hotel room has hired a lawyer to prepare civil legal action. Law firm Slater and Gordon confirmed on Saturday morning that it had been engaged to investigate a potential civil claim on behalf of the woman, and lawyer Jackson Pannam said the woman was “trying to navigate an incredibly traumatic experience”. The Pullman East Melbourne hotel, where the Swans players stayed on Sunday night. Simon Schluter He said his client called the police “immediately after what had happened” in the early hours of Monday morning at the Pullman East Melbourne hotel. “She’s provided a statement and she’s continuing to assist the police with their investigation,” Pannam said.



Related Article Analysis

AFL off-field behaviour Nobody knows if any of these five will play for the Swans again “Whatever the outcome of the criminal investigation, we intend to explore other avenues for our clients to seek justice, including through civil remedies, we will be putting all of the relevant parties on notice in due course.” Pannam told reporters the woman’s complaint to police was about “alleged sexual assaults”. A police spokesperson, in a statement on Saturday morning, said Sexual Crimes Squad detectives continued “to investigate a report of a sexual assault”. “The exact circumstances of the matter are still being established and a number of people have been spoken to,” the spokesperson said.



“As the investigation remains active and ongoing, we will not be commenting further including providing information on the specific circumstances of the matter, movements of detectives and any statements or interviews taken.” This masthead has previously reported that star player Isaac Heeney is at the centre of the police inquiry. Sydney Swans players (from left) James Jordon, Chad Warner, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey have been suspended for the rest of the season. Nine Five Swans players – Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey – were stood down for the rest of the season for breaching the club’s standards. On Friday, a lawyer representing the other two women who were present at the hotel on Monday described what occurred as “demeaning, abhorrent and simply not moral or acceptable”.



Related Article Exclusive

AFL off-field behaviour Swans hotel drama deepens as former star placed inside late-night party “These women were subjected to the most disgusting actions and behaviour I have ever heard about in my 28 years as a lawyer,” Carbone Lawyers head of personal injury and litigation John Karantzis told 3AW. Karantzis also claimed there were “even a few leaders in that room” along with the five Swans players. Pannam described those comments as unhelpful, and said the woman he represented had not yet spoken to the media and wanted privacy. “I’m not in the business of ranking the types of cases that I’ve been involved in,” he said.



“Certainly, I don’t think that’s helpful.” The Swans have denied there were any other club officials or staff members in the hotel room. “The Sydney Swans supports the action taken by Victoria Police in releasing today’s statement regarding the investigation,” the club said on Saturday. Loading “The Sydney Swans categorically confirms that no member of staff is involved in the investigation. This includes being in the hotel room central to the police investigation.



“The club reiterates that no player has been interviewed by police at this stage.”



Pannam, when asked who his client intended to launch legal action against, said: “A claim for compensation can be made against anyone who has caused or contributed to someone suffering injury, harm, damage. It’s very early days, and we are considering our options. “We’ll be writing to the relevant parties in due course with a view to putting them on notice of what our intentions are.” Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Qld child safety watchdog barks over lack of progress. Minister says state is acting
World.content:
PoliticsQueenslandQueensland government Qld child safety watchdog barks over lack of progress. Minister says state is acting Matt Dennien August 22, 2026 — 1:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A senior government minister says Queenslanders can have confidence in the path ahead for the child safety system, despite a key watchdog raising concerns about reduced transparency and a lack of change. Principal Queensland Family and Child Commissioner Luke Twyford made comments to News Corp after Child Safety Minister Amanda Camm axed an annual survey of children in state care. Twyford said this made Queensland’s child safety system “one of the least transparent” and its operations “invisible”. He also described the lack of change felt by children as “a shocking performance assessment”. Queensland Family and Child Commissioner Luke Twyford with Attorney-General Deb Frecklington in June. Courtney Kruk The Crisafulli government came to power promising change, but Camm has faced issues around the rollout of a long-awaited IT system, a growing number of kids in residential care, and reduced funding.



A government-commissioned inquiry was cut short, and Twyford’s commission was to be absorbed into a new body. This also came amid concerns about changes to adoption practices. When asked on Saturday about Twyford’s comments, Education Minister John-Paul Langbroek said he respected his views. “We do work closely together with Luke Twyford in my portfolio, but also via the attorney-general and the police minister and the child safety minister, and we respect his views absolutely,” Langbroek said at a press conference on the Gold Coast. Asked if Queenslanders could have confidence in a system that the watchdog could not properly monitor, the minister did not give a direct answer. “Queenslanders can have confidence that we have a way forward and a road map following the royal commission and the recommendations that we continue to implement,” he said.



Related Article Queensland government Child safety system ‘broken’, Camm admits, revealing rising number of kids in care “I’d reject that we’re not doing things quickly enough. It’s a very big job, and it’s after 10 years of neglect from the former Labor government.” Langbroek also ruled out government action against Twyford for his comments. “Of course he’s entitled to his views, which we’ll always take into account,” he said. Despite Camm praising the last My Life In Care results in 2024, the decision to scrap the survey has been attributed to the fact the former government gave gift cards to participating children. Child protection bodies, including the Family and Child Commission, had said such payments were best practice to ensure children were thanked for taking part.



A departmental spokesperson quoted by News Corp would not say whether the government was planning to launch an alternative to the survey. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: AFL LIVE: Lethal says Pies should take decision out of Pendles’ hands; Blues in charge at Marvel
World.content:
AFL great Leigh Matthews says it would be wrong for Collingwood to allow Scott Pendlebury to make his own call on his playing future, declaring the Magpies needed to deliver honest feedback.

Pendlebury, 38, was hurt in the Magpies’ 63-point loss to Brisbane on Friday night, finishing the contest on the bench with a knee bursa issue, that is swelling near the joint.

Scott Pendlebury walks from the ground with his Collingwood playing future in doubt. Getty Images

The Magpies also have concerns the former skipper has a hamstring strain, scans to confirm whether he has any chance to play in next weekend’s wildcard round.

Should Pendlebury not play and the Magpies lose, the league’s all-time games record holder may have suited up for the last time at Collingwood, for he does not have a contract for next season.

He is set to become an unrestricted free agent, with several clubs linked to his services if he opts to play elsewhere in 2027.

Magpies president Barry Carp said on Friday night that the choice was in Pendlebury’s hands, but Matthews, the 1990 Magpies premiership coach, said any decision should largely be the club’s call.

“Not in my opinion, it’s never the player’s call,” Matthews told 3AW on Saturday.

“But Scott Pendlebury is a high-class person. If [coach] Craig McRae and the football people said: ‘We think it’s probably time’, I think he would accept that. And that’s the way the conversation should go.

“But a player just can’t say: ‘I want to play, I don’t care if you don’t think I am up to it, I just want to play and I want a contract.’

“But even Barry Carp, I don’t think he would go that far. I think if the football department said: ‘No, we just think it’s time’, I probably suspect Scott Pendlebury would accept that himself.

“It’s a joint conversation but it can’t be unilaterally the player decides, otherwise he would play until he is 50.“

Pendlebury has said if his body feels fine, he would commit to playing on. The Gold Coast Suns and Essendon have been linked to the two-time premiership player, the latter in a deal which could have him become an assistant coach.

Matthews said the Magpies’ coaches would need to be honest with Pendlebury.

“It should be a choice but sometimes players have to be told what you are observing from those who are running the team,” Matthews said. “You try to do it diplomatically but you also have to be honest and say, and use Scott as an example: ‘We think it’s time, we don’t want to be playing half a year in the reserves’, for instance. I think most players would accept that from their coaches.

The Magpies will play either Carlton or the Western Bulldogs next weekend. Pendlebury’s finals campaign last year ended early in the preliminary final when he strained a calf.

World.title: ‘Scorched earth for satire’: How this former ambassador’s show was scuppered by Trump
World.content:
Exclusive NationalComedy ‘Scorched earth for satire’: How this former ambassador’s show was scuppered by Trump Stephen Brook August 22, 2026 — 1:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Diplomats never tell, but a new dark TV comedy created by the former Australian ambassador to France promises to be anything but discreet. Brendan Berne, our man in Paris from 2017 to 2020, has just filmed the pilot for a sitcom called Rank, inspired by his two decades of service with the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade. Brendan Berne (left), pictured with French President Emmanuel Macron, is a former ambassador now focused on creative projects. Berne, 56, who resigned from DFAT in 2020 to move to Burgundy in France with his husband and to concentrate on creative projects, describes Rank as “The Thick of It updated for the age of Trump, Truss and Thunberg”. Networks and production houses were interested, but then the US president sued the BBC for defamation and, long story short, corporations shied away from a pointed comedy in the era of Donald Trump, Liz Truss’ short stint as UK prime minister and eco-warrior Greta Thunberg.



“Trump suing the BBC has scorched the earth for political satire, and the joke invigilators and sensitivity readers make transgressive comedy challenging. Five years on, someone laughed it’s been my Odyssey, but I’d say it’s more been the Plodyssey,” Berne says. “When the rights returned to me, I revisited my more provocative scripts, which resonated with investors, and we have just finished shooting the pilot.” As Australia’s ambassador, Berne helped to persuade French President Emmanuel Macron to visit Australia – a first. And in 2017, when Australia’s marriage equality legislation became law, he started a video on social media discussing stronger relations between Australia and France and ended it with him proposing to his Swiss-Australian partner of 11 years, Thomas Marti. Millions in France viewed it on social media, which led to Berne appearing on France’s top TV talk show. Rank is not Berne’s only project. He has helped to develop a cello concerto that tells the largely lost story of a 19th-century French cabin boy being adopted by an Aboriginal tribe on the Cape York Peninsula.



Melissa King, the director of artistic planning for the Sydney Symphony Orchestra (SSO), commissioned the work, by composer Matthew Hindson. It was developed with the support of the Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies and is scheduled to premiere in NAIDOC Week next year. The concerto will bring to life the largely untold story of 14-year-old Narcisse Pelletier, who was abandoned by his ship’s crew in Far North Queensland in 1858 and adopted by the Uutaalnganu people, with whom he lived for 17 years. The cast of Rank (from left): Phillip Honeywell, Bryan Williams, Felicity Bown, Jodyanne Fletcher Richardson, Dana Blacklake and Will Frazer. “This an important concerto for the SSO, as it brings the story of Narcisse and the Uutaalnganu to a wider audience, the first major cultural project dedicated to this incredible true story,” King says. Berne and French cellist Sebastien Hurtaud, who hails from the same place as Pelletier, travelled last September to the Cape York Peninsula and met members of the Uutaalnganu people, some of whom still had oral accounts of Pelletier passed down from the 19th century. While visiting, Hurtaud played part of the composition for locals.



“They still share stories of the para (white man) who they saved in 1858 and who became part of them. One young woman recounted to me the story of Narcisse killing a crocodile after it had taken a baby, earning the respect of his new community,” Berne says. Pelletier was later returned to France against his wishes, and his parents forced him to undertake an exorcism. Berne (right) and husband Thomas Marti in Paris. “As a former ambassador to France, I believed this forgotten chapter of the France-Australia relationship needed to be told, especially as the Indigenous people were the hero of the story,” Berne says. “I also hoped it might help salve some of the wounds in the immediate wake of the cancellation of the submarine program in a country where culture means a tremendous amount.”



The French embassy in Australia appointed Berne to the French-Australian Culture Exchange Foundation, which is chaired in Melbourne by Myriam Boisbouvier-Wylie. Related Article Foreign relations Trump, subs and the Iran war: Australia’s replacement for Rudd has arrived in DC Berne’s TV program had a circuitous route to existence. In 2022, it was ranked in the top three of a co-production pitching competition, Series Mania, an international TV industry festival staged annually in Lille. In developing the project, he worked with executive producer Glen Condie, the Emmy Award-nominated producer of Top End Wedding. Rank, billed as a comedy of diplomatic proportions, was written by Berne and should appeal to disillusioned Gen Xers. It is set in a fictional South Pacific country, where British diplomats decide to give asylum to a rogue state weapons scientist in a misguided attempt to celebrate women in science week. The team is then thrown into turmoil by the appearance of a bumbling British minister.



The program will be released in December and is available on rankthecomedy.com. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘On the next adventure’: Renovators sell inner-city Edwardian for $1,385,000
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions ‘On the next adventure’: Renovators sell inner-city Edwardian for $1,385,000 Wes Mountain August 22, 2026 — 1:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A two-bedroom Edwardian in Richmond, directly across from Bicentennial Park, sold for $1,385,000 at auction on Saturday – $65,000 above its reserve. The home at 20 Parkville Street sits in a row of red-brick terraces looking onto the park. It maintains original exterior features such as tessellated tile paths and stained-glass windows, and has an updated interior featuring high ceilings, open-plan living and new appliances. It had a price guide of $1.2 million to $1.32 million, and a reserve of $1.32 million. Jellis Craig Richmond agent and auctioneer Luke Schickerling said strong bidding opened at $1.2 million, the bottom of the guide, and went up quickly in $10,000 increments before hitting $1.32 million and being declared on the market.



Related Article Exclusive

Melbourne house prices How much it costs to live in Melbourne’s most desired school zones From there, three potential buyers continued to trade bids until the home sold to a young couple, who Schickerling said were new to the Richmond area. The vendors were renovators, who he said were now “onto the next adventure”. He said the property had performed well, and there were more people bidding than he would have expected just a few weeks ago, as the market was starting to warm up for spring – traditionally the peak period for auctions in Melbourne – and fewer properties were coming up for sale than expected. “We have the lowest stock levels I can recall in recent memory,” Schickerling said. The preserved Edwardian features at the front of the property conceal a modern, spacious interior. Jellis Craig Richmond



The property was one of 598 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne this week. In Brunswick, a warehouse conversion apartment – in the same building known to be the home of Nina Proudman in the TV series Offspring – sold for $1,126,000 at auction, soaring $126,000 above its $1 million reserve. The light-filled two-bedroom apartment at 210/1-3 Dods Street, complete with quirky egg-yolk yellow central bathroom, expansive open-plan living, dining and storage areas, and a north-facing view to Brunswick’s churches and rooftops, had a price guide of $950,000 to $1 million. Nelson Alexander Brunswick agent Janine Ballantyne said auctioneer James Pilliner opened bidding at $970,000, before four bidders pushed it easily past the $1 million mark in $10,000 increments.



From there, the bidders winnowed down to three to take the price up to $1.1 million, and then down to two as the increments grew smaller and the auction came to a close. The buyer was a professional moving into the area. The egg-yolk yellow central bathroom, askew in its own box within the apartment’s expansive interior, was just one characterful element of the warehouse conversion. Nelson Alexander Brunswick The vendor had decided to upsize within Brunswick after 21 years in the stylish apartment. Ballantyne said the result was indicative of the market. “[It’s] price-sensitive, but if people can see value, they will engage,” she said. “It doesn’t feel as though we are going to have the usual levels of spring stock, whether that puts pressure on prices or not remains to be seen.”
